speakeroldname: Hon. Roger C. Simmons (Burin-St. George's) moved
speechtext:
that Bill C-405, an act to amend the Income Tax Act (tax credits for disabled senior citizens), be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee in the Economics envelope.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I want to begin by telling you about a friend of mine, Tommy LaFitte. Tommy lives in a community in my riding called Port au Port near Ste-phenville. Tommy and I talk about fishing. We talk about hunting. We talk about the Blue Jays.

Occasionally Tommy and I speak French, because he is a francophone. His father settled in Newfoundland, and Tommy was born in a small village near Stephenville.

Tommy and I have known each other for less than three years. We met in August 1990, and since then we have become very good friends. As I said we talk about many things. We do one or two things together. Let me say that a year or so after we met, Tommy and I, together with a member of his family because Tommy is not the kind of fellow his family wanted to let loose in Toronto all by himself, went off to Toronto to the SkyDome to see a Blue Jays game.
What does this little anecdote have to do with the bill before us? Tommy LaFitte, and this is something I have not said up to this point, will very shortly celebrate his
102nd birthday. Tommy and I and his son Stan went to the SkyDome to celebrate his 100th birthday. I first met him when he was 99 years of age.
Tommy LaFitte expects to live many more years. He made a promise to some people at the SkyDome, the vice-president of the Blue Jays, that he would be back on his 110th birthday. Knowing Tommy, I fully expect he will be there.
Tommy LaFitte may not need the provisions of this particular bill. Tommy is pretty spry as I have just indicated. He has all his faculties, both mental and physical. He still enjoys a big birthday party of several hundred people every year. He likes to chat in either language about his 73 years as a fisherman, his years as a hunter, and his passionate interest in the Blue Jays. He can quote statistics of the better players on that team, and it has some good ones. Tommy may never have occasion to draw on the kinds of provisions we are proposing in this bill.
Tommy has a loving family around him. He has support through his son, through his daughter-in-law and through an extended family which keeps in close touch with him and visits him often. They look after not only his physical needs but see to it that he has good emotional support.
There are a lot of Tommys out there. Equally there are a lot of people out there as old as Tommy or certainly in that general age category but without family support, without financial resources and without the physical and mental stamina Tommy enjoys at 102 years of age.
It is that other group of people I would like to talk about this morning. Bill C-405 is concise and to the point, and so it should be. It proposes that a disabled senior citizen or a person who has a disabled senior citizen as a dependant be permitted to deduct from tax which would be otherwise payable an amount equal to 75 per cent of the disabled senior citizen's defined medical expenses, home help expenses and transportation expenses. In short it would allow disabled seniors to deduct certain taxes to assist them with the business of getting on with their lives.

May 10, 1993
Private Members' Business
It is worth noting that this bill reflects one of the principles that the Standing Committee on Human Rights and the Status of Disabled Persons presented in its report to the House just a few short weeks ago. One of the principles stated in the report last month was that the taxes which people with disabilities pay should be reduced by measures that offset their disability related costs.
The budget presented by my friend, the Minister of Finance, in 1991 made some significant moves in the right direction on this issue by increasing the disability tax credit from $575 to $700 for 1991 which represents altogether a tax credit of $1,085 if provincial tax is taken into account. It is a move in the right direction, and for that we applaud the minister and the administration.
However the government's action, if I may say so to the minister, has not been sufficient in all cases to allow the disabled to recover the share of their income consumed by their disability. This is particularly true of seniors with disabilities. Hence this bill. That is the reason we have it this morning.
Maybe we ought to look at a few facts which should help us in coming to the right decision on the proposal contained in this bill. We know, for example, that nearly half the people 65 and over and 8 out of 10 of the people 85 years old and over have some form of disability.
Elderly people with disabilities are severely limited in the range of normal activities they are able to pursue because of economic and environmental barriers. They are restrained, constrained and limited by economics, by lack of dollars and by environmental physical considerations.
Eighteen per cent of all seniors who need wheelchairs do not have them. One in five seniors who have need of a wheelchair do not have one. In this country, in this day and age with our reputation for affluence, with our reputation for humanity, with our well earned reputation for assisting those in need, it is mind-boggling that our fellow Canadians are having their physical movements restricted, limited, simply because they do not have wheelchairs to get from point a to point b. We are talking Canada 1993.
Twenty-nine per cent of seniors with disabilities need special features to help them move around their own
homes, such as walkers and so on, and they do not have them. More than one in four people are prisoners within their own homes, prisoners of a particular room because we have not helped them get that simple device to get from one room to the other, from the bedroom to the bathroom, from the living room to the kitchen. Twenty-nine per cent of disabled people find themselves in that category. That too is shameful.
Elderly Canadians with disabilities also have problems using public transportation. Twenty-five per cent of the people who have access to public transportation have difficulty using it because of their disabilities.
The story goes on. I have a few more facts before I come to the real point of this bill. Hearing and vision problems are also common among elderly people.
Did members know that 31 per cent of the seniors with hearing disabilities are in need of hearing devices which they do not have? One in three in that category could have their hearing capability improved if he or she had a simple hearing device. Do they know that 10 per cent of them need visual aids such as glasses, et cetera, and do not have them?
In this country in 1993 significant proportions of elderly people with disabilities require some assistance with their daily living activities. For example, 34 per cent need assistance shopping. Another third need assistance with housework. Eighteen per cent need help preparing their meals and 15 per cent need help with personal care matters.
That is what this bill is about. It is to reach out to those groups of people to help them do some of the things they cannot do for themselves. If we look at the older in that group, the people 85 years of age and over, 66 per cent of them with a disability need help shopping and 57 per cent need help with their housework.
I believe already I have said enough to demonstrate there is a need. There is a large body of people out there who could be helped by this bill, who could be assisted greatly if we allowed them to deduct from tax that would otherwise be payable those medical expenses, those home help expenses, those transportation expenses proposed in the bill.

May 10, 1993

There will be those who will say we cannot do it. It is too expensive. I ask them, before they put their foot in that one, to have a look at the bill and at the facts which relate. The bill places some reasonable limits. We will not have seniors being able to get taxis every day of the week and then deducting it from taxes that would be payable. That is not the case. If we read the definitions in the bill we find this is a very plausible proposal that will meet a need without getting out of hand in terms of the public costs that might be involved.
The first half is that there is a need, and that I have said. The other half is that the people we are talking about find themselves with fairly low incomes.
It has been found by StatsCanada in the last little while that the incomes of elderly Canadians with disabilities are relatively low. For example, 60 per cent of them with disabilities have incomes below $10,000. Income problems, we should note, are particularly severe among elderly women who have disabilities. One group that is having a particularly rough time is elderly women who have disabilities. We have to do what we can to make life a little easier for those people in particular, and we can do it by passing this legislation today.
Housing affordability is also an issue for many seniors with disabilities. In short, many barriers still affect the lives of a significant share of our disabled elderly population. The further reduction and eradication of these barriers will help the aging population in Canada to pursue productive and active lives.
I feel very strongly about this issue. I would hope my colleagues in the Chamber will see fit to give this a leg up for seniors with disabilities. They can do it very simply by allowing this bill to go to committee at the end of the hour debate.
In conclusion, we have it in our hands to do the right thing. The right thing is very obvious and is not difficult to do. Let us not be side-tracked by arguments that it is going to cost a bundle of money. I have had it costed and it will not cost a bundle of money. That is not the issue.
The issue is one of humaneness. The issue is one of fairness. The issue is one of conscience, whether we can allow to go on any longer what is going on, where senior
Private Members' Business
disabled people, including in particular senior disabled women, are having a rough time simply because we have not put in place legislation that is sufficiently humane.
My appeal this morning to colleagues in the House is to take this one small step to make life just a little easier for these people.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to support Bill C-405. The New Democratic Party would like very much for this bill to receive second reading and be referred to a committee for more detailed study. There are aspects of it we would like to take a look at in committee, and we might make some suggestions for improvements.
The principle of this bill has a lot of merit. In 1991 the census showed that 4.1 million Canadians, or 15.5 per cent, were disabled. But when one looked at the age group 65 and over, that figure showed that 46 per cent of all seniors 65 and over were disabled. Of that number, 31 per cent were severely disabled, meaning they would have difficulty performing daily functions, using public transportation and caring for themselves.
When one looks at earning an income we find that 70 per cent of the total population is normally employed. But when one looks at the disabled population, that figure drops down to 40 per cent, and even that 40 per cent is quite misleading when one looks at the gender differentiation. The 40 per cent breaks down into 30 per cent for women and 49 per cent for men. Sixty per cent of those who are employed and disabled make less than $10,000 a year.
One of the things that we would like to have looked at in committee is whether the bill should be broadened to include not only disabled persons over the age of 65 but all people who have disabilities. They face additional hardship and cost because of their disabilities.
This legislation talks about additional medical expenses. That is fairly clear, particularly when one includes within the definition of medical expenses some of the newer technologies that are available to assist the disabled, everything from telephone adaptations to assist people who are hearing impaired to a whole variety of mobility devices from wheel walkers to sit-down walkers to motorized wheelchairs designed to assist those who are disabled and unable to get around like the general population.

May 10, 1993
Private Members' Business
There is a discussion of home help. One of the things that makes it very difficult for many disabled to remain independent and in their own homes and out of the institutions which end up costing the taxpayers a great deal more money is the fact that they cannot care for themselves adequately.
They need assistance in daily routines within their own homes. These daily routines may simply be heavy cleaning or doing the weekly washing, but it may also include preparing meals, shopping, doing minor maintenance around the home and assisting them even in getting in and out of a wheelchair or into bed. It would not cost taxpayers if we provided some tax relief to these people, allowing them to remain independent in their own homes. In fact it could be a considerable cost savings.
Another area mentioned is transportation. Last week I held a series of coffee parties in my riding. One couple phoned my office and asked if we could provide them with transportation. Both of them were disabled and they had not been out of their home since Christmas because they could not afford specialized transportation. They depended on neighbours and friends even to get out to try to shop.
When we examine some of the issues we should be looking at in committee, particularly if the committee broadens its thrust so that it looks at extending this bill not only to those 65 and over but to all disabled people, one thing we should be examining is the participation rate of disabled people within the employment market. Even in our Canadian Jobs Strategy program the participation rate of disabled people has fallen dramatically in the last two years or three years. In 1987-88 the participation rate was about 4.2 per cent. By January 1992 it was down to 1.6 per cent.
This federal government has cut $100 million annually for training from each of the two budgets. We talk about private industry picking up the cost of training, particularly for the disabled, and yet we know that the private sector provides only 25 per cent of gross domestic product for training, compared to twice that amount spent in the United States and four times in Britain and Germany. We have to develop and emphasize employment equity programs to assist the disabled to move into the employment market.
The federal government introduced employment equity legislation in 1986, but of course it had no teeth. It was only a reporting piece of legislation. The government even exempted itself and its direct employees from having to report. We should contrast this with what the Government of Ontario has done. In 1992 it introduced mandatory employment equity legislation. It has goals and timetables to make sure that it really happens. However some companion legislation and changes from the federal government are required and this is one of them, to allow for tax deductibility for these expenses.
In my last minute I would like to comment on what the government side is going to say: Where are we going to get the money? Let me suggest that it could do away with some of the expense allowances for corporate executives.
In Vancouver they are in the process of building a new hockey rink. I wonder how much of that is going to be financed by tax dollars for box seats by the multinationals, big companies and the wealthy, in that they can write them off in their taxes. It would be much better if we gave a tax break to the disabled rather than to the wealthy and the corporations.
This government has extended the Liberal mistake on family trusts for the wealthy. It would be much better to give a tax break to disabled men and women than to give and continue a tax break for wealthy families.
The question is not whether there are funds available, but what choices we have. Too often over the last number of years governments have chosen to give tax breaks to the wealthy and the powerful corporations. I say they should be giving them to the more deserving disabled.

speakeroldname: Mr. Marcel R. Tremblay (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Prime Minister; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance; Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)
speechtext:
Private Members' Business
I would like to start by thanking the hon. member for raising the issue of the tax treatment of senior citizens. This government shares the hon. member's concerns, especially about the tax treatment of disabled senior citizens.
However, the proposal before us today in Bill C-405 also raises a number of practical problems. One problem is that this proposal would not apply to recipients of the disability tax credit under the age of 65. Although senior citizens are more likely to be eligible for the disability tax credit-nearly 40 per cent of those who claim the credit are over 65-all individuals eligible for the senior citizens tax credit, whatever their age, must live with serious deficiencies.
Individuals are eligible for the disability tax credit if, as a result of their disability, they are markedly restricted in their activities of daily living. This criterion identifies a deficiency as serious if its effect is equivalent to that of being blind or being confined to a wheelchair. Since age is already a consideration when determining eligibility for a disability tax credit, there is no reason to provide additional tax benefits based on the age of recipients of the disability tax credit.
I also want to point out that our tax system already allows for the effect of age on the ability to pay of senior citizens in this country. It does that through the age credit and the pension income credit. In 1993 the age credit reduces federal and provincial income tax of individuals over 65 by approximately $915. Persons receiving a pension income from a private plan may also claim the $1,000 credit for pension income, which reduces federal and provincial income tax by up to $260.
Altogether, disabled senior citizens receive up to $2,290 in tax relief from the federal and provincial governments. However, disabled individuals under 65 receive a total of approximately $1,120, or less than half the amount disabled senior citizens would receive.
Another problem raised by Bill C-405 is the very high subsidy it would provide to those who are eligible for the tax credit. This raises concerns about fairness to other taxpayers and also about the potential for excessive use of medical products and services. This problem has two aspects. First, the proposal would allow senior citizens eligible for the disability tax credit to claim the full amount of expenses incurred. However, both in Canada and the United States, tax relief only applies to costs over and above a certain percentage of the claimant's net income.
In 1993 the federal Medical Expense Tax Credit allows the taxpayer to deduct 17 per cent of eligible medical expenses in excess of the lesser of $1,614 or 3 per cent of the individual's net income. The 3 per cent rule is used to restrict the tax credit to medical expenses over and above normal health care expenses in Canadian households. In the United States, the tax relief applies only to expenses in excess of 7.5 per cent of net income.
The second and by far most important reason why the proposed subsidy may be too high is that a 75 per cent federal tax credit results in a real subsidy of over 115 per cent, if we consider the impact on provincial income tax.
The government realizes that the needs of disabled senior citizens are important. However, I am sure hon. members will agree that a subsidy for more than 100 per cent of expenses does not make sense. It would merely encourage unnecessary expenses incurred for equally unnecessary or inappropriate treatments. And all Canadian taxpayers would have to make up this substantial revenue shortfall.
In fact, the question arises whether the tax system is the right mechanism for providing the kind of subsidy intended by Bill C-405. After all, the tax system's main objective is to obtain revenues from the public in as fair a manner as possible, so that the government can fulfil its mandate to offer the products and services that are part of the Canadian social fabric.
Measures like the disability tax credit, the medical expense tax credit and the age credit add to the fairness of the personal income tax system. The purpose of these measures is not to subsidize senior citizens and the disabled but to provide tax relief based on the impact that age, the seriousness of a disability and exceptional medical expenses have on the individual's ability to pay taxes. That is why these credits are set at a rate of 17 per cent, the initial marginal tax rate at the federal level.
That being said, I would like to point out that, on the basis of a number of factors, we can assume that generally expenses related to the disability of persons who claim both the disability tax credit and the medical expenses tax credit are almost entirely compensated for under the tax system. It is estimated that individuals who claim both the disability tax credit and the medical expenses tax credit received about $212 million in tax relief in 1989. According to data taken from the Statistics Canada Health and Activity Limitation Survey, disabili-

May 10, 1993
Private Members' Business
ty-related expenditures were evaluated at about $226 million.
As far as government spending is concerned, I may remind the hon. member that provincial programs offer substantial subsidies to senior citizens and the disabled, and that the federal government-through the Canada Assistance Plan-shares in the cost of these programs. The programs subsidize a considerable part of the cost of prescription drugs, functional equipment and accessories, family help services, auxiliary services and nursing care. If implemented, the proposals described in Bill C-405 would clearly overlap benefits provided by these programs and might result in a reduction in the benefits they offer.
I believe that existing measures constitute a better response to the needs of senior citizens and the disabled than the proposal described in Bill C-405. We are, of course, open to suggestions and new ideas for improving our response to the needs of these people and helping them, but I may remind the hon. member that we are not starting from scratch. Any new proposal should, of course, allow for existing measures and for what the government has already done to meet the needs of its citizens.
In concluding, I must say that because of serious practical problems associated with the measures proposed in Bill C-405, I find it hard to support them. Consequently, my only option is to ask hon. members to reject this bill.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to begin by congratulating my colleague from Burin-St. George's who, like many Liberal leaders before him, has shown a consistent attitude when it comes to looking after and being sensitive to the needs of senior citizens.
Canadians forget but it was in 1927 that Liberal Prime Minister Mackenzie King introduced the old age pension. It was in 1957 that Louis St. Laurent developed Canada's first RRSP program. In 1966 Pearson changed the age of eligibility to 65. As well in 1966 Pearson introduced the Canada Pension Plan, medicare and the guaranteed income. In 1969 John Thmer, then Minister
of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, amended the Patent Act to allow the sale of low cost, no name drugs to seniors. We all know that in 1972 Pierre Trudeau indexed the old age pension an'd eventually brought in quarterly indexing.
The member for Burin-St. George's is following in the Liberal tradition of making sure seniors are looked after.
What amazed me today when listening to the Conservative Party was the member saying: "We have concerns with this bill because it does not deal with the disabled people who are under 65". This is something we can deal with in committee. I cannot believe we should not give the same approach to disabled people in all walks of life. This is one of the many inequities of our tax system.
Three weeks ago we passed a bill in the House that extended our ability to do any kind of taxing of private family pensions, family trusts and private trusts to the tune of billions of dollars. We have extended indefinitely the period where we have access to them in terms of revenue. One of the reasons the government gave was that these families might have disabled children who would have to be looked after. That is one of the reasons it brought in the bill to continue the family trust.
Twenty-one years ago it was a Liberal initiative. We stood in this House this year and said it was time to review this. Times have changed, and here is the government using children from disabled families as a reason to extend it.
Today we are talking about a condition in our country where we want to look after seniors who may need to deduct from their income expenses relating to their disability and the government is walking away from allowing this to go to committee for refinement and enhancement. I find this absolutely unbelievable. On the eve of an election the government has declared war once again, declaring to the senior citizens of Canada that it is not going to discuss it.
There is another reason. We now have the GST. We now have four million people out of work. The litany goes on and on. Now we find the government will not allow this bill to go to committee. Who are we talking about? We are talking about disabled senior citizens who will incur expenses beyond $1,000. My colleague from Burin-St. George's is asking whether it is fair for a senior citizen who incurs an additional $1,000, $2,000,
May 10, 1993

$3,000 or maybe even $5,000 and wants to deduct this from his or her income. It is beyond my imagination that this Conservative government is not allowing it to go to committee. I cannot believe there is a person in Canada who would be so insensitive to discussing this matter. The cost today for some of the new services and items that we have to help look after our disabled people is well beyond $1,000.
Is the government really serious? One-fifth of our senior citizens cannot afford a wheelchair. My colleague from Burin-St. George's says we have to look after that one-fifth and the government is saying it does not want to discuss it. One-third cannot afford hearing aids and the government does not want to discuss it. It does not make sense.
Governance is not for the advantaged. We are here to look out for those in our community who are disadvantaged. My colleague from Burin-St. George's stood in this House today and put forward a constructive bill which would help look after disadvantaged senior citizens in our community.
We are not talking about senior citizens who have millions and billions of dollars in family trusts. We are talking about disabled senior citizens, asking whether a way can be organized so they can get a tax deduction for the extra expenses they incur because of their disabilities. The Conservative government is saying it does not want to discuss it. It does not think it is a good idea.
We are in opposition right now and there is not a lot we can do about it. The government in the last two to three years has allowed all kinds of tax expenditures for foreign multinationals or has allowed tax expenditures to sit on the books of major corporations. It is not that I have any disrespect for the contributions that corporations make in terms of job creation. Two years ago there were 2,200 corporations in this country with retained earnings in excess of $25 million, not counting companies with losses carried forward. These 2,200 companies did not pay a nickel's worth of taxes because of the tax expenditures buried in our inefficient, unfair, complicated tax act. The government did not do anything about it.
Private Members' Business
My colleague from Burin-St. George's is calling upon the government today and bringing to the attention of the House that among our senior citizens are many who are disabled, who cannot afford to have hearing aids. They cannot afford wheelchairs. They need help in terms of their transportation. Let us get this bill to committee so that we can discuss it and maybe develop a tax expenditure. This would be a cost to the Treasury of Canada, but I challenge any Canadian who is listening to this debate to pick up the phone and say the Conservative government is right, that we should not be looking after those disabled people whose expenses because of their disability are beyond $2,000. If there are any Canadians who are like that they are certainly not in my community. If they are in my community they are certainly not Liberals.
I sit here in total bewilderment. Once again I am dumbfounded the Conservative government, on the eve of an election, is so unco-operative with seniors.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to rise today to speak in support of Bill C-405 which the hon. member for Burin-St. George's has put forward. This is an incredibly good bill.
It would not be necessary if the present government had concern. The government of the last eight years made nothing but little piecemeal token gestures to the disabled community and almost none to those in the senior community who have disabilities. It is very necessary.
The points covered here, such as the cost of transportation for seniors and the cost of home care for seniors, can be just absolutely unmanageable for most Canadian families. It is really too bad we have to bring this bill forward, but it is long overdue. Things we have not been able to get to in the disability committee are included in here. I certainly hope the Conservative government will change its mind and at least see fit to let this go to committee so it can be studied further.
I want to make a few comments about persons in Canada with disabilities. We know now there are over four million Canadians living with some kind of disability. That is well over 16 per cent of our total population.

May 10,1993
Private Members' Business
It is not a small group of people we are talking about. Many of these disabled persons are seniors.
We can all think of a senior we know who has difficulty seeing, hearing or walking, maybe a parent, grandmother, friend or neighbour. We all know, and some of us are closer to it than others, we are all going to be in that position shortly. As the population ages there are going to be more and more people in this area. As we get older we develop more disabilities and we need help from the government. As Liberals we feel that is what the government is for, to help those who cannot help themselves. If this segment of the population needs help then we should be helping them.
As an example of how the Liberals are always concerned about people who cannot look after themselves and making sure that they are well looked after, in 1981 the Standing Committee on Human Rights and the Status of Disabled chaired by the Hon. David Smith, a fine Liberal who brought in the Obstacles report, really covered every area that needed to be covered for the disabled, including seniors. There were 130 recommendations in that report. That was in 1981. Twelve years later very few of these recommendations have been acted upon. I have to give credit to the committee. The committee has been trying and trying to put forward suggestions but this Conservative government has just not followed through on them.
In 1990 the committee put forward a report A Consensus of Action. It had a lot of suggestions for the government with regard to economic integration and helping the seniors community. The government rejected five of the six recommendations in the report. This Conservative government is really not concerned about helping those who cannot help themselves.
The standing committee took probably an unprecedented action and wrote another report to the government saying it did not like its answer to the first report. The government then came forward and said it would put out $158 million for the disabled. This is to be spread over a five-year period to 10 different departments. This is for over four million disabled Canadians. It worked out to $1 a year for each disabled person. That is not veiy much money to help a disabled person with their transportation and home care costs. It was $1 a person for the disabled community.
The government made a big fanfare and a lot of noise about all the money it was putting out. It is over 16 per cent of our population and they get $1 a year for their special problems. This shows how much the government is concerned about it.
The government did bring out an omnibus bill but the disabled communities across the country were very disappointed in it. It may have been too much of a build-up. It had been working on it for quite a number of years. There was very little in the report and there was nothing in particular for senior citizens.
I spent two years travelling across the country with this report, which is available to the public, called Recommendations for Change. We discussed right across Canada the problems of the disabled. It is not just that they need a little bit here and a little bit there and help with some other problem there. The whole system has to be changed so the disabled are covered, no matter what their age. This bill is fantastic because it specifically says the seniors need special help in special areas. Let us give it to them.
It would be fantastic if the government were to suggest that instead of this bill discussing things that can be done for disabled senior citizens it should apply to all disabled citizens in Canada. The government would defray their transportation expenses for weekly shopping trips or visits to the doctor. Home care costs should also be defrayed. Therefore it would be equal for all Canadians with disabilities. However there is no chance the government is going to do anything for all disabled people in Canada.

speechtext:
There are two motions in amendment standing on the Notice Paper in the name of the hon. member for Moncton for the report stage of Bill C-112, an act to amend the Excise Tax Act, the Access to Information Act, the Canada Pension Plan, the Custom Act, the Federal Court Act, the Income Tax Act, the Tax Court of Canada Act, the Tax Rebate Discounting Act, the Unemployment Insurance Act and a related act.

Motion No. 1 will be debated and voted on separately.
Motion No. 2 goes beyond the scope of Bill C-112 since it would introduce a new concept. The Chair must rule it out of order, according to paragraph 698(1) of the sixth edition of Beauchesne. Therefore it will not be selected.

I shall now propose Motion No. 1 to the House.

Motion No. 1.
That Bill C-112 be amended in Clause 12 by adding immediately
after line 15 at page 28 the following:
"(1.1) Section 128 of the said Act is further amended by adding immediately after subsection (1) thereof the following:
(1.1) For the purposes of paragraph (l)(b), a co-operative corporation which is a registrant resident in Canada is a prescribed corporation in relation to a co-operative corporation which is a shareholder of it, where
(a)	not less than 90% of its shares are owned by co-operative corporations, and
(b)	not less than 50% of supplies made by it are made to co-operative corporations that are shareholders of it."
He said: Mr. Speaker, this is a very specific amendment. This bill smoothes out all the bumps and wrinkles that have been associated with the administration of the GST.
This amendment deals with a situation involving cooperatives. Co-operatives are experiencing a unique situation setting them outside what was contemplated by the legislation. Hopefully the government will adopt this amendment in order to correct the anomaly.
It is difficult to describe. Let me explain it using the example of a major chain store or grocery store that has a number of stores across the country. If the head office does things for its branches throughout the country, if it provides services such as accounting, advertising and other types of head office functions, it is an expense of the company.
What happens with co-ops, however, is that when the head office, the regional or provincial general offices do work for its member co-ops it attracts GST. Each thing done by the central co-op for its member co-ops will require the central co-op to charge GST. The member co-op will be required to pay the GST and then apply to

May 10, 1993
Government Orders
the government for a refund. The end result is that the accountants do well. All the professionals do well. Computer people do well trying to design a program to administer it. The net effect is that the government does not get any more money because the money has to be remitted back to the member co-ops. Therefore all that is created is bureaucracy.
The minister shakes his head saying that this is crazy, that this legislation is crazy. This amendment will do something to address the idiotic position in which this government has put co-ops.
How would your GST work?

Wait till you see. It is going to be an exciting moment for you fellows when you see how well we can administer it.
I will tell them this much. We will certainly not have the bureaucracy and the mess that have been created. Look at the size of this bill and the amendments. Is this performance? I do not think so.
In essence the purpose of this amendment is to put some fairness into an unfair tax system called the GST. It will at least be fair to the co-ops so they are not competing on an unlevel playing field. Clearly that is the circumstance now. They have to hire extra people just to collect the tax, remit it and then get it back.
The purpose of this amendment is very simple. It is easy to understand and one's eyes will not even get tired while reading it. When it is all done it will do something for the co-op movement. I take great pleasure in putting forward this amendment. I am sure that at least rural Conservative government members will see their way clear to support the co-op movement and support co-ops throughout-
And the urban ones too.

The urban ones as well, but with this government we never know for sure. I hope at least the rural members will see the benefit of supporting the co-op movement. Maybe some of the urban members do not understand that there are urban co-ops as well and that they make a contribution to our business community-
Without further ado, that is the purpose of the amendment. It is something that is needed and something which I hope will get support all around.

speakeroldname: Mr. Marcel R. Tremblay (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Prime Minister; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance; Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government recognizes the contribution of co-operatives to our economy and society. It believes this form of enterprise plays an important role in Canada's economic and social growth.
The government has recognized some of the unique characteristics of the co-operative sector in the design of the GST. Under the GST special treatment has been afforded financial co-operatives and co-operative shares. I would like to say a few words on Motion No. 1 relating to co-op sales. I will divide my comments into five different topics.
First I would like to say that in addition to the special treatment co-operatives have already been given under the GST, the co-operative movement is asking that sales between co-ops be zero rated. When the GST was first introduced there were numerous similar requests from various groups of businesses. However, paying tax on purchases and claiming input tax credits is fundamental to the way that a value added tax works. As with any exception, making an exception to the rules increases compliance and administration costs for registrants and the government.
The only exception made to the general rule was in the case of sales between a parent corporation and its wholly owned subsidiary. This recognized that the subsidiary was really like a division of one company.
Abandoning that criteria as in the case of co-ops would in effect be abandoning the basic structure of the GST. It would throw open the door to countless other requests for the same exceptional treatment for any group of companies which in some manner were related to one another.
This motion will open the door to a variety of requests. We have made just one exception up to now for companies and their wholly owned subsidiaries. This motion will open that door and the results will be costly when considering the administrative costs in dealing with the various requests.
May 10, 1993

speakeroldname: Mr. Marcel R. TYemblay (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Prime Minister; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance; Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to move third reading of Bill C-112.
Government Orders
Bill C-112 contains several important refinements to the GST. These refinements will help to ensure the continued smooth and efficient operation of the tax.
I would like to briefly address some of the amendments contained in this bill and how they improve the operation of the GST. To begin, let me note that with a major tax reform such as the replacement of the federal sales tax with the GST, there will occasionally be a need to fine tune the system. The proposed amendments before us today are based on the practical experience of seeing the tax at work in the marketplace. They have been developed through extensive consultations with businesses, organizations, tax professionals and individuals.
That being said, this legislation will not significantly alter the general operation of the GST. Rather, the bill proposes important technical amendments to simplify GST compliance for particular sectors of the Canadian economy. As a result, these industries can turn their efforts to the important business of creating economic growth.
Bill C-112's measures relating to the Canadian taxicab industry are a prime example of the practical nature of the proposals contained in the bill. The operation of the GST would be amended to enable the taxicab industry to operate nationwide under a consistent pricing structure. A uniform price structure will entail significant administrative savings for this industry.
Along similar lines, the government received constructive representations from direct selling organizations. As a result of these discussions, the government is proposing new rules under which tens of thousands of independent sales contractors of direct sellers will not have to register and file GST returns.
On this last point, I would like to note that, during the legislative committee debate on this bill, amendments were proposed to further simplify the operation of the tax for direct sellers. I am pleased to report that these amendments were approved by the committee and are included in Bill C-112 for consideration by hon. members today.
Bill C-112 also contains benefits for retailers. The amendments would simplify the operation of the tax for a wide variety of special types of transactions, ranging from the treatment of discount coupons to the treatment fo returnable beverage containers. Moreover, simplified rules have been designed specifically for retailers who make purchases through buying groups. The new rules, which are supported by associations representing man-

May 10, 1993
Government Orders
ufacturers and distributors of grocery products, will significantly reduce the required paperwork.
Simplifying the GST for business is an important objective of the government. That is why Bill C-112 contains measures that would allow for greater flexibility with respect to reporting requirements for up to one million businesses. In particular, Bill C-112 would make it easier for these businesses to file GST returns only once a year. As a result, they can devote more time to earning profits and less time to paperwork.
Bill C-112 also introduces changes that will simplify the operation of the GST in areas where activities are often undertaken by joint ventures. This is particularly relevant for the oil and gas industry, which has voiced its support for the legislation.
Another group that will benefit from this legislation is auctioneers. Bill C-112 will allow auctioneers to follow a consistent accounting procedure for all of their transactions. This is what associations representing auctioneers across the contry told us that their members needed and this is what the government has proposed.
The government has also worked to improve the competitive position of service exporters by allowing them to import certain goods for servicing without having to pay tax on the importation. Similarly, Canadian international competitiveness will also be strengthened by refinements to the GST treatment of sales of goods and services by Canadian companies to foreign customers.
As we heard in committee, many of these new rules are of particular benefit to auto parts manufacturers in southern Ontario centres such as Windsor and Oshawa.
I would also note that the treatment of exports-in particular, legal services provided to foreign companies-was an issue on which the legislative committee reviewing this bill heard representations. The committee recommended refinements that are reflected in the bill before hon. members today.
In addition, the bill provides broader relief under the tourist and foreign convention rebate program. Let me remind my hon. colleagues that Canada's program is already unequalled among other countries that have similar tax systems. By helping to maintain the attractiveness of Canada as a destination for foreign visitors and convention organizers, this change would further enhance the competitiveness of our tourism and convention industry.
The bill also contains provisions that will benefit Canadian farmers. To that end, the government has consulted with farmers and is now proposing a relieving amendment that will bring the GST treatment of livestock feedlots into line with that of feed mills and other suppliers of tax free livestock feed. As well, farmers will be provided with broader cash flow relief on their purchases of bagged fertilizer. This is particularly beneficial to farmers in remote areas.
On a broader level, Bill C-112 would make the GST fairer for all businesses. The legislation provides for discretion on the part of the Minister of National Revenue to waive penalty and interest in cases where a person is unable to file a return or make a remittance on time due to extraoardinary circumstances beyond the person's control.
The legislation also contains proposals that would yield direct benefit to Canadian consumers, particularly those in need. For example, the bill contains proposed additions to the list of tax free medical devices and prescription drugs. In addition, it provides that Canadians living year-round in travel trailers would be allowed to rent their sites in trailer parks on a tax exempt basis. This ensures that these Canadians are treated the same as other residential tenants. The bill also provides a simpler, more generous GST housing rebate to individuals who build their own homes.
Finally, the government is proposing a special credit for certified institutions that employ mentally or physically disabled individuals in the manufacturing of goods. This credit was designed in recognition of the unusually high costs faced by these institutions during the transition to the GST.
In closing, let me reiterate that this bill will improve, simplify and increase the fairness of the GST. This legislation is the result of extensive consultations with businesses, organizations, individual Canadians and their professional advisors. The government has worked together with them to identify specific problems in particular areas of the GST, and has proposed workable solutions that are tailored to the realities of today's marketplace.
May 10, 1993

Tax professionals have studied and applauded this legislation. They have urged its speedy passage in order to reduce uncertainty in the application of the tax.
Mr. Speaker, I echo their counsel and ask all members to give their full support to this bill.

Mr. Speaker, it certainly sounds from the government's perspective that this bill is a cure-all for all things that ail the tax system in Canada. I do not think we on this side can go quite so far.
As everyone knows we are fundamentally opposed to the GST and the system that is in place. We are looking at ways to improve the tax system and make it fairer for Canadians. At the same time we are faced with some amendments that on their face, if we accept the GST, are satisfactory and in order, although a lot of them do not go far enough and do not do the job properly. We are faced with the conundrum of having to deal with amendments that are improving a bad piece of legislation called the GST. We do not have any choice at this particular stage but to try to work within the system which the government has created and see if there are ways we can make it better.
During committee and throughout much of the discussion with respect to this particular bill we heard from a number of groups, but the government had closed its mind to any amendments or changes which would have been of any benefit. We saw that attitude again this morning with its position on co-operatives.
The co-operative situation is very simple and straightforward. I find it really unique that lawyers came to our committee and wanted an exemption for lawyers who are hearing foreign arbitrations. This government bent over backward to accommodate the lawyers to make sure they did not have a hard time and that foreign arbitrations would not attract GST. When it comes to helping out Canadians and co-operatives the government has a closed mind. It is not prepared to do anything to support co-operatives.
Government Orders
The simple amendment which was proposed and voted down this morning would have just added fairness to the system. The other amendment which was ruled out of order was another simple matter that would have put a level playing-field between direct selling co-operatives and other grocery store operations.
Direct selling co-ops charge a service fee every week of approximately $3.50. There is no question it is not a major item, but the government requires the members to pay GST on the $3.50 each week. That is manifestly unfair. A large portion of the purchases are food purchases that do not attract GST. Therefore Loblaws, Sobey's or any of the other facilities have a benefit to the detriment of the co-op movement and the direct selling co-operative store.
The minister says to get serious. We have been trying to get serious with this legislation and help people who are in need. His attitude is to close the door and make it more difficult for co-operatives and the people who are at the base level trying to help other people. The minister should take another look at his government's position rather than support it in this particular fashion.
Another serious aspect to this bill that one has to take a look at is its retroactivity. This is tax legislation and the government is going to make it retroactive to January 1991, which was quite some time ago. Small businesses are now going to have to figure out whether they are caught within this retroactivity or not, how it is going to work, and what they will have to do. They will have to fill out forms and deal with the bureaucracy to handle the retroactivity outlined in clause 210 of the bill.
At committee we urged the government to take another look at it. We said there was something fundamentally wrong with the approach it was taking. It was putting the small business community at jeopardy because of the retroactivity of the particular legislation. The government has a closed mind about things that come from the opposite side and refused to even entertain a change in the retroactive aspects of the bill.
The government is prepared to look after the lawyers who happen to be doing some foreign arbitration, but it is not prepared to look after small business. It is not prepared to make life a little easier for the small business community which is the backbone of our economy.

May 10,1993
Government Orders
There is another dangerous trend in the bill as well. It is with respect to access to information. I refer specifically to clauses 128 and 211. The commissioner wrote asking us not to enact the legislation as it presently exists but to make changes to allow for more freedom of access to information. Again the government had a closed mind and said it was not prepared to look at it. It was not prepared to make those changes, and so again another opportunity to add a little more fairness to the situation and have a little more information available for all concerned was lost.
It is an interesting situation. If one looks at the bill one sees that these are amendments. This is not GST legislation per se but amendments to legislation. If one looks at the explanatory notes they indicate clearly it is like a novel, except it is very dull reading. It might replace Sominex or something like that. The documentation is massive.
Small businesses are trying to figure out what they are supposed to do with the GST. I would like to read one section I find fascinating because if you can figure it out, Mr. Speaker, maybe there is another career opportunity for you.
I am referring to clause 46(2). It goes on a great length and then says:
(f) where the particular person is a registrant who was entitled to claim an input tax credit, or a rebate under Division VI, in respect of the acquisition of the property or service, the particular person shall be deemed, for the purposes of this Part, to have made a taxable supply and to have collected, at that time, tax in respect of the supply equal to the amount determined by the formula A times B over C times D -
That part is easy. It goes on and says:
-where
A is the tax fraction,
B is the input tax credit or rebate under Division VT that the particular person was entitled to claim in respect of the acquisition of the property or service,
C is the tax payable by the particular person in respect of the acquisition of the property or service, and
D is the amount of the rebate paid to the particular person by the registrant.
I am sure you are excited, Mr. Speaker, about hearing this type of easy to understand, easy to read legislation that this government is putting forward to help small business function in our economy today.
As much as I like accountants I think all we have done is draft about 400 pages of legislation to make accountants richer with no real benefit, no value added, to the economy or the business community at all. In fact it is a major detriment.
These types of examples are sprinkled throughout all the legislation. This government has made a very complex piece of legislation even more complex. It has made it harder for Canadians to understand. Businesses think they are going to have some improvements with this legislation and they are going to be surprised when they actually see how it comes into effect.
The bill deals with a number of things, but as a general statement I will say that we all now know the GST was the wrong tax. The government was committed to it and it cannot go back. One reason we should change governments is so we can rectify this problem.
What are you going to do? Tell us what you are going to do.

What are we going to do? We are going to get rid of the GST.
The GST collected $30 billion in revenue. Thirty billion dollars came into the coffers of the government. As a result of all the administrative costs and the rebate the government netted $15 billion. Fifty cents on every tax dollar that comes into the coffers through the GST go out in the way of rebates or expenses. They look at that, try to justify it and say the tax is working, but the simple fact of the matter is that if we did not have the rebates and all the administration we could probably lower the GST to 3 per cent. Instead this government hangs on with all the nonsense of amendment upon amendment, changes and an increase in the bureaucracy. No wonder we have to spend as much money as we do.
Then the government forces GST down people's throats when the provinces have systems in place that could have avoided the redundancy of the federal GST administration. However this government does not want to work with the provinces. It forces through this legislation and now these amendments which are further complications to an already complicated circumstance.
May 10, 1993

We all know this piece of legislation called the GST has not generated what it was intended to generate. There has been a huge shortfall. The government was anticipating this would be a great windfall and, as it has turned out, it has generated about $7 billion less than what it expected.
We never said that.

I can remember all the arguments indicating that it was going to generate at least $18 billion, if not $22 billion a year net, and it came in at $15 billion. The minister is using the same system the Minister of Finance uses when he does his budgets. They do not even come close to the numbers.
Get the facts right.

I have the facts right. I remember exactly what the Minister of Finance said when he implemented this tax. He said this would generate large sums of money and it has fallen short by billions. Now the government says that really was not what was intended.
It sounds exactly like the Minister of Finance with his budget estimates when he said they would reduce the deficit. It was to go down to $27 billion but it turned out that it went up by $1.1 billion to $35 billion. That is the kind of mathematics the government functions with.
What is serious about the GST is that in addition to everything else it has driven the economy underground. There is a huge economy flourishing underground. If the government wants to understand why it has not been able to achieve the revenues it expected, the reason in large measure is that it has driven the economy underground. It is still flourishing there but we are not collecting any revenues.
There was a recent article in The Globe and Mail talking about the number of cheaters within the GST system. We all know that is going on. We try to put our heads in the sand and say, as the minister just said, that it is not true; but it is true.
We have a system of taxation that is driving the economy underground. It drove us into a far deeper recession than we had anticipated. Now the government is going to add more complexity and more complications to an already overburdened system. The main focus is
Government Orders
against small business. It will create another handicap for small business that is not faced by small business in any other country.
The amendments are probably in large measure acceptable because they improve on a very bad tax, but the improvement on the bad tax does not improve the bad tax. It is the system that has to be changed and it will be changed in a few months.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to join the debate this morning. I found it curious my Liberal colleague did not answer the questions posed to him by the member opposite, the minister of state for finance, as to what the Liberals would do in the event that they actually kept their promise of getting rid of the GST. They have been very vague on that particular point.
No, no. You have been very vague.

No, I think we have been very clear about how we think we could replace the GST. We would do so mostly by closing Liberal tax loopholes the Conservatives have yet to close.
It seemed the Liberals were almost ready to make a policy statement at one point, I forget how many months ago, about a new tax that would have included food. The word got out and a great blanket of silence fell over the land. That rumour was only out for a few days.
Tell that to Bob Rae in Ontario.

We got them going. They are obviously very sensitive on this point. The truth hurts because the truth is that the Liberals plan to go parading around the country saying that they intend to get rid of the GST. What they intend to replace it with will remain a secret, a very well-kept secret, until that allegedly happy day comes when they are, as they hope, elected. Then the Canadian people will find out what they intend to replace the GST with.
Unfortunately for the Liberals the blanket of silence came a few days too late, and it is not the most well-kept secret in the country. We know they are contemplating some kind of tax that might be even more heinous than the GST, if one could imagine such a tax, in so far as it would include food.

May 10, 1993
Government Orders
Perhaps the next Liberal who rises, if there is to be one, could elaborate on the question asked by the minister of state for finance as to just what the Liberals would do. The Liberal member who was just heckling me suggested we had not said what we would do. We have.
I have put out a document, as the NDP tax critic, explaining how we feel we could get rid of the GST. I will admit there are many things in there that some people might object to, but it is an alternative policy. I know the minister of state for finance would object to some of the things we have in our alternatives to the GST, but at least we have something we can debate. He could then get up and say that he thinks we are wrong on the business and entertainment tax deduction and that eliminating it would hurt the restaurant industry.
I could say that I do not think it would, that where it has been eliminated in other places the restaurant industry has not been hurt in the way it thought it might. However the minister of state for finance and myself have something to argue about. There are a number of other tax measures that we could talk about and that I may even talk about today.
When it comes to the Liberals what are we to talk about? What are we to debate? All we have is the rhetoric of opposition to the GST, but no real suggestion as to what the Liberals would do. It is certainly not going to be closing tax loopholes because many times last year I raised the whole question of the bill that the government introduced to extend the capital gains tax exemption on private trusts. Was that ever raised in the House of Commons by the Liberals prior to the bill being introduced, or for that matter even after the bill was introduced?
It was not even until committee that the Liberals finally cottoned on that maybe there was something here on which they should get on side with the NDP and oppose. Previous to that there had been no mention of it in the House, no questions asked in Question Period. Indeed, when the bill was debated at second reading the Liberals were still very much in favour of that particular part of the bill. Their critic actually got up and thanked the Minister of Finance for clarifying the matter in a way that would permit them to continue to support the government measure. They later changed their minds but it was a little late.
One of the things that has already been mentioned but merits repetition with respect to the bill is the way in which the government seemed to go out of its way to be helpful to lawyers and accountants who appeared before the committee but resisted every attempt to try to change the rules with respect to co-operatives. I heard
the minister of state for finance say something. Maybe when he gets up he could explain why the government has not been willing to meet the needs of the co-ops in this regard and create a level playing-field between themselves and other retail stores.
On the face of it this would be a fair thing to do. I do not understand why the government would continue to stonewall the co-op movement on this issue unless-and this is entirely possible-it has a philosophical objection to co-operatives because they do not operate in that purely entrepreneurial, rugged, individualistic and private enterprise way that the Conservatives idolize. Maybe this is the objection. Maybe it is an attempt to penalize the co-op movement for not conforming to the dominant ideology. I am not sure. Maybe the minister of state could clear that up. I would just like to reiterate the question of co-operatives and the fact that the government refused to consider amendments which would have helped in that regard.
The whole question of access to information has been mentioned and the fact that the government has moved to further exempt the Excise Tax Act from the Access to Information Act. Again we see that even the commissioner, Mr. Grace, is concerned about this particular provision. This is the second time in not so short a period where the government has been caught out by its own commissioners who have particular concerns. Here the information commissioner is concerned about something the government is doing.
It was not so long ago, with Bill C-921 believe, where the privacy commissioner was concerned about a measure that the government was bringing in with respect to the ability to access the tax files of Revenue Canada employees. One would think the government would be more sensitive to this kind of criticism, and that if a commissioner indicated a concern the matter would either be postponed or some way would be found to deal with it. In the case of Bill C-92 it looked as if it was going to be dealt with, as the offending clause was withdrawn from the bill in committee but reinserted later at report stage exactly as it had been.
May 10, 1993

Government Orders
In the meantime the government has been able to persuade the privacy commissioner that its regulations would somehow deal with this problem. We hope that is right, but I have to confess I am sceptical. This is another example of the government going against the advice of people who have the specific responsibility of concerning themselves with particular matters, in this case the Access to Information Act.
Curiously enough the provisions with respect to the Access to Information Act are going to be retroactive. I am not sure how that is going to work. What about the information which has already been accessed? Does the government have a plan for somehow rolling back time and recovering the information which has already become public? This would seem to be a new dimension of arrogance on the part of the government. In any event it raises the larger question of the retroactivity of the other measures in the bill, and that is a matter that has also been mentioned as a concern.
I was speaking earlier about the whole question of the GST and the commitment of the NDP to getting rid of it. We feel it could be done. First it has to be considered that the GST itself costs money. It is not a question of recovering that which the GST brings in. It is a question of recovering what the GST brings in over and above what would be saved by not having the GST in the first place. It costs money to collect the GST. The GST has an effect on inflation. Inflation has an effect on other government programs. It is a more complicated scenario than people tend to give it credit for when they are thinking about how difficult it might be to replace the GST. Certainly it would not be easy, but we did have a GST-free Canada until a few years ago.
I am certain if there were the political will we could have a GST-free Canada again. It might take some real political will to make the tax system more fair and more progressive, to collect some of the money out there that is not being collected as a result of various tax expenditures, loopholes, shelters, whatever, making the system more progressive as a whole. There are ways in which this could be done but they would have to be comprehensive. I will admit to the government there is no single alternative tax measure that could be adopted which would replace the GST. It would have to be a package of measures. We think that package could be constructed.
We might end up, if we were doing it, with people angry with us. We would have the people who benefit from these various Liberal tax loopholes which were put in there in the 1970s angry with us. However the people of Canada would not be angry with us because they would be glad to be rid of this particular tax.
I will tell members who would be most glad this moment. It would be the housing industry. The front page of the Winnipeg Free Press today is full of stories about how the new housing industry is being sorely curtailed by the GST because people are much more wont than they used to be to buy an older home or just a home which has already been built. It does not have to be particularly old in order to avoid paying the GST. That may be true with respect to car sales as well. I am not sure. I have not seen any statistics on it.
The way the GST is applied it is certainly a great incentive to not buy a new house. The construction industry estimates that the job losses in Winnipeg alone have been quite significant as a result of the GST.
I also see in the paper this morning an ad about GST cheating costs. It is costing the government $2.3 billion a year, says an Ontario report. What have we done? If there is that kind of cheating going on across the board, we have moved from a system in which there was a considerable degree of things working on the honour of Canadians to a system which is now discredited to the point where we have more of an underground economy. We have more cheating as this article states. It is very much to be regretted that both the substance of the tax and the way in which it was brought in have done a lot to discredit the entire tax system.
Elements of that tax system deserve to be discredited. I am speaking of elements which existed before the GST. The fact is that regardless of what we think about particular tax measures this country and other democratic and civilized countries, so to speak, depend on a certain degree of willing compliance on the part of citizens with the tax system. Otherwise we would need either an outlaw tax system or a police state in order to supervise it all.

May 10, 1993
Government Orders
Anything which undermines and erodes people's commitment to dealing with the tax system fairly, honestly and in a mood of willing compliance is something that ought to concern the government. I hope it does concern the government. Maybe the minister of state for finance will want to comment on that as well.
It will be an awful legacy on the part of the current government if we are able to look back some years from now and say it was this point in time when people's confidence in the tax system as a result of the GST began to erode and eventually led to a situation of massive tax avoidance of an ordinary nature by a great many Canadians.
For all these reasons we continue to oppose the GST. We continue to oppose bills like the one we have before us which merely tinker with that tax instead of eliminate altogether.

speakeroldname: Mr. Marcel R. Tbemblay (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Prime Minister; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance; Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the legislative review committee put forward, as the hon. member mentioned, an amendment dealing with litigation services. This was in response to representations made by the Canadian Bar Association to the committee explaining that certain charges could undermine the process that Canada has made as being recognized as a preferred place for resolving certain international disputes.
As I said to the hon. member, the amendment made at committee improved the bill by ensuring that Canada's competitiveness in this area is not threatened. I am surprised my hon. colleague disagrees with enhancing Canada's competitiveness in that way.
He also made reference to access to information on the GST. Nothing in this bill restrains the access of any interested person to general information about the GST. Indeed the government has made every effort and will continue to make every effort to inform the public about the tax from the release of the first white paper in 1987.
Subsequent technical papers and numerous technical information bulletins were released by the government to make as much information available as possible. The bill ensures information on specific taxpayers is protected as taxpayers rightly expect their privacy to be protected. However, general information about the tax
will continue to be open to the public. An amendment to this bill will clarify that only taxpayers' specific information is protected.

Mr. Speaker, I will deal with the last point first. I presume the member is aware that confidential and personal information with respect to the excise tax is already exempt. It seemed to us that the government had not given good enough reasons for going beyond that. Maybe he might want to explain just what it is the government is trying to exempt.
Second, with respect to the representations of the Canadian Bar Association, I was not so much opposing what the government did as contrasting what the government did in that respect with the representations that have been made to the government repeatedly by the co-op movement to have a level playing-field so that it can stay competitive with its retail competitor.
The government is very interested in creating a level playing-field for lawyers doing foreign litigation, but when it comes to something like the co-op movement wanting a level playing-field with respect to its competitors, the government has a deaf ear. As I say, it was a matter of contrast rather than comment on the particular amendment.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the member for Winnipeg Transcona why if his party is obviously opposed to the GST his leader indicated that it would take their party five years to abolish the GST, whereas the Liberal Party has indicated that it would do away with it within one year.
If the GST in the eyes of the NDP is like a malignancy, why would it be five years? This defies common understanding. If in fact the GST is truly as bad as we believe in the Liberal Party and we would do away with it in a year, why would it take the NDP five years?

Mr. Speaker, the difference is that we actually intend to get rid of the GST. People who do not intend to get rid of the GST can say anything they like. They obviously do not intend to get rid of it, and that is why they say the things they do.
In our jobs plan, which many Canadians are reading with approval, we outline how we can get rid of the GST and replace the revenue it now raises through a series of improvements in the tax system, many of which I spoke about earlier.
May 10, 1993

Mr. Speaker, Bill C-112 contains the changes proposed in the notice of Ways and Means Motion of December 9, 1992. Much of it concerns changes to the goods and services , tax but there are also some rather technical measures. Since my colleagues mentioned it earlier, I would like to point out two of our concerns.

I am concerned about certain measures in Bill C-112 that would exempt information on the goods and services tax from access to information.
The information commissioner, Mr. John Grace, raised concern about clauses 128 and 211 of the bill. He is concerned that the government is giving itself total control over release of any GST information. He referred specifically to a complaint being investigated by his office that Revenue Canada tried to block release of the list of GST registrants.
Revenue Canada, in fairness and in response to that concern, said that these amendments would not prevent individuals from determining whether a vendor was registered for GST purposes. Revenue Canada says that these changes are intended to restrict the disclosure of taxpayer specific information in a way that parallels section 241 of the Income Tax Act.
The government assures us that we will still have access to information on the administration of the GST. I among others will hold it to this assurance. The information commissioner is also concerned, and this is the main point, that these amendments could restrict his office's ability to investigate complaints.
The government has not responded to the information commissioner's specific concerns. We do not know yet if the changes the information commissioner suggested in his submission to the finance committee will be adopted. If they are not then I submit there is a serious concern on the part of the information commissioner, shared by many Canadians. It will remain to be seen whether we can put to rest this concern as soon as possible.
On a more specific measure in Bill C-112 affecting section 167 of the Excise Tax Act, I would like to highlight something which is a little closer to home in my
Government Orders
case, having been a practising chiropractor for some 35 years.
Under the existing act, the sale of business assets of all chiropractic practices would attract GST including that portion which we call goodwill that is in the name and reputation of the practice. The change in Bill C-112 to section 167 will mean that the portion which is goodwill will not be GST taxable when the business is primarily involved in making exempt supplies. The supply of chiropractic services is exempt when rendered to an individual.
Furthermore the amount charged for the supply of goodwill will not be considered in determining whether a business is a small supplier or required to register for the GST. This is minor but of importance to some of my colleagues in the profession.

Mr. Speaker, on listening to the government-and I would like to return to the whole of Bill C-112-one might believe that these changes to the GST would make this tax, which is hated in Canada, function better and more efficiently.
Here we are, three years later, with 350 pages of simplifications to the GST. Just months before an election, the government proposes a 350-page bill to simplify one of the most hated taxes in Canada. As I will try to prove, it is a complex tax which is costly to administer and which imposes a heavy paperwork burden on small business.
The parliamentary secretary and member for Terrebonne, in his speech on second reading, said on page 16901 of Hansard:
- these measures represent a rigorous fine-tuning of the details of
the tax. They simplify GST compliance across many sectors of the
economy.
