Mr. Speaker, let us see if the GST is easy to administer. The Auditor General, Denis Desautels, and the minister of revenue disagree on the annual costs of administering the GST. It is an honest disagreement. They do not agree on the figures, even on those which should be quoted.
The Public Accounts of Canada contain some gems. Mr. Speaker, you need only consult these accounts and you will find all these figures that I am giving you for

May 10, 1993
Government Orders
1991-92. The gross revenue forecast for 1991-92 was $29,495,478,000, while net revenue, as we said earlier, was about $15.2 billion. If we deduct the administrative costs of about $486.1 million, which we have not yet done, we are left with a net balance of $14,682,361,000. As the member for Moncton said before, we thus lose nearly 50 per cent of the gross revenue from the GST in administering it and giving refunds.
I could compare the tax with the old federal sales tax, but time is short and if I get a question, I will tiy to enlighten the member who asks me about it. This situation is different, but it is still good to look at it and useful to compare with past experiences.
Let us return to the concern with efficiency and effectiveness. It is quite difficult even for a well-informed person involved with the issue to find or obtain information on the administration of the GST. It is hard to reconcile the details in the public accounts and the departmental expenditure bulletins. Nevertheless, the departments, especially the department of revenue, have the information. For example, I will give you a classic case that happened recently.
According to documents given to the public accounts committee recently by Revenue Canada, the revenue department alone spent $339.6 million administering the GST in 1991-92. The public accounts for the same year contain the same figure of $339.6 million, but that is to administer all taxes, including the GST, the goods and services tax.
Why the confusion? The parliamentary secretary told us in his speech that the government wanted to make the GST simpler and fairer. They should also make it clearer and make the information easier to understand.
I take a classic example: coding industries. For example, we would like to know how much the GST brings in on clothes or books or all sorts of other goods or services.
The information on industries was not requested on the registration forms. Industrial classification began in mid-1991. Detailed revenue information on the GST is essential for Canadians. If we want to assess the program, we must ask if this assessment planned for 1994 will be available if the coding itself is not complete until 1994.
If we want to know if the tax is equitable, we should know how it is applied, to whom and on what it applies.

A great number of amendments to the GST, as demonstrated by Bill C-112, show there are an awful lot of things to be corrected if this tax is to work at all. Over the last several months I and others have learned a certain amount about the GST. This learning has left me with many questions and doubts about the administration of this tax.
It has been said that a little learning is a dangerous thing. If the government would only provide us with the information we seek, look for and ask for, perhaps we could remedy my thirst for knowledge on the GST.
The best thing to do with the GST as far as I am concerned, and this I share with my Liberal colleagues on this side, is for the next government, and I hope it will be a Liberal government, to replace this tax with a fairer tax. A fairer tax would be one that applies in an equitable manner, one that is efficient and effective.
Tell us how.
I hear the government minister over there saying: "Tell us how".
That is rhetoric.

It is not rhetoric. It is a question you just put to me: "Tell us how". Listen attentively, Mr. Minister, about dismantling.
In the first session of the new Parliament Liberals will mandate the Commons finance committee to consult Canadians and provincial governments on all the options to the current GST. The current Minister of Transport is mouthing something. If he wants to ask me a question I would be more than happy to answer him after I have finished my speech. If he wants to know what we are going to do he should listen.
I will repeat. In the first session of Parliament we will mandate the Standing Committee on Finance to consult Canadians and provincial governments on all the options to the current GST and to report within 12 months.
May 10, 1993

Our objective is clear, to replace the GST in a way that generates equivalent revenues, is fair to consumers, easier to administer for small business and promotes federal-provincial co-operation.
The government put in the GST without any consultation. I hear the minister over there saying why should Canadians not say they like the GST. He either has not been with it or he has been somewhere else. If he goes across the country he will find out that the GST is the most hated tax Canadians were ever asked to pay. The best thing to do as far as my party and I are concerned is to replace the GST.
We learn not surprisingly that apparently there is a great deal of GST cheating going on. In The Ottawa Citizen dated April 21, 1993 is an article about a leaked International Monetary Fund report on the Canadian economy. According to this report the Minister of Finance and his colleagues who were appearing before the board told the IMF that compliance with the GST had been surprisingly poor. This is one reason why revenues are less than forecast and why federal finances are in the bad shape they are today.
A few minutes ago the minister of privatization said that somebody on this side did not tell him how much the government had anticipated raising in revenues from the GST. I will tell him because it is all public. It is all in the budget documents. The minister did not know so I will tell him.

The revenue forecast for 1991 was $16,350 million dollars; the expected revenue according to the budget of February 25, 1992 was $16,400 million and actual revenue according to the Public Accounts for 1991-92 was $15.2 billion.
Mr. Speaker, they were off. None of their predictions turned out correct. They are unable to count.

I believe we are dealing with a serious matter when we talk about the hidden economy. I believe there is an underground economy in Canada which is mining revenues. It has been estimated the size of this underground economy ranges between 5 per cent and 20 per cent of Canada's economy. It is a huge figure. In 1985 the current Minister of Communications who was then Minister of National Revenue-it was not me who said
Government Orders
it; I see the minister for privatization and the Minister of Transport laughing-estimated the size of the underground economy to be $40 billion, with a resulting loss of tax revenue to the government of $9 billion a year.
The Tories' answer-and again I hear the ministers over there laughing-has been to spend more money. The average cost per GST registrant with 1.9 million registered right now went up to $179.64 in 1992-93 from $150.92 in 1991-92. Is it because of enforcement or collection difficulties? Why did the price go up?
This means the government spent $60 million more last year to administer the GST than the year before. Is that a fair and efficient tax? Is it reaching its effective goals? Rather than fixing the problem to make the tax fairer and more acceptable to Canadians, the Tory government threw money at cracking down on cheaters.
The GST has undermined Canadians' confidence in the fairness of our tax system. It is understandable. It prolonged and deepened the severe recession we are experiencing and encouraged Canadians to stop spending, which caused our economy to grind to a halt. In the recent budget we learned the Tories were again penalizing the poor by reducing GST payments to twice a year from four times a year just to improve their balance sheet.
In January 1994 a payment of $625 million will be due to people who paid GST and will be entitled to a credit. The government put it off until April 1, 1994, thereby reducing its 1993-94 deficit by $625 million. However the 1994-95 budget will be increased by an account payable of $625 million. That is what we call playing with the books. Anybody in the private sector with an account payable would declare it and in this case pay it, but not this government.
The GST in general is a burden on Canadians, but it is also a burden on small business. I want to address that question. It is costly to administer, expensive and time consuming for small businesses. The Canadian Federation of Independent Business, a renowned and respected organization, conducted a survey of 25,362 businesses. It found that on average a small business had to spend almost $4,000 in one-time costs to implement the GST into its operations. Complying with the GST cost each small business on average $5,158 in 1991. On to this we

May 10, 1993
Government Orders
can add the government's cost of about $180 per registrant for a total of $5,338.
The federation says the cost of compliance for small business appears to have dropped 30 per cent in 1992 from a total cost of $6.6 billion in 1991 compared to $4.6 billion in 1992. However we slice it, this is still a heavy burden on small businesses which are the engines of growth for an economy like ours.
Furthermore many public servants are required to administer the GST. Revenue Canada says-and this is official-it took 3,960 persons at a cost of $486.1 million for 1991-92 to administer and collect the GST. Of this amount $330.6 million was spent by Revenue Canada, $54.9 million for the administration of the GST credit and $91.6 million by other departments.
I could go on to compare the GST with its predecessor, but I will avoid that because I do not think it is too constructive. The federal sales tax of the day caused some problems. It was replaced but the GST is a bad tax. It was badly set up. It was put in at the wrong time. This government should know that Canadians are going to throw it out, not only for the GST but for all the other things it did to Canadians. There have been 34 increases in taxes since it took power.
I could go on and talk about the projected net revenues of the government and the budget it cannot get straight. These people cannot shoot straight, let alone count. We have proposed that at the next Parliament to get rid of the GST. That is a promise we will keep. I hope Canadians will remember the harm the government has caused this country with the GST.

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to the comments of my hon. friend from Ottawa- Vanier on the GST. We could debate this at some length.
As I understand it, the Liberal's program is called trust us. It says: "We are going to wipe out the GST within a year. We are going to send the Standing Committee on Finance across the country to get the ideas of people on what the tax should be instead of the GST and we will implement it within a year". That is what I understand my hon. friend to say.
It is my understanding, and you can correct me if I am wrong, Mr. Speaker, that the Liberals did this four times. They had a wonderful opportunity with two royal commissions on the economy. Two standing committees went across this country and did that. Every one of them suggested they wipe out the manufacturers' sales tax, which the Liberals did not do although they had that advice for 40 years running. The recommendations on most of them was to bring in a value added tax which the goods and services tax is.
I want to ask my hon. friend a direct question. If he does go across the country with members of the standing committee and finds that the GST is the fairest value added tax we can have in this country, would the Liberals change their minds and not wipe out the GST?

Mr. Speaker, we are all laughing at that question. The hypothetical question to be asked is: Does the minister go out into the country and find out from Canadians what they think about the GST? That is the question to be asked.
How do you do that?
What do they think about the GST? They think it is a lousy tax.
Oh, oh.

Let me finish. Our goal is clear. I will say this slowly so it will not be misunderstood. We must replace the GST with something that generates equivalent revenues, is fairer to consumers, easier to administer for small business and others, and promotes federal-provincial co-operation by replacing the present system.
I will just read an editorial from today's The Ottawa Citizen:
Canadians who believe their national finances are in the hands of competent, private enterprise trained Tory managers should examine their records more closely.
Consider, for instance, the goods and services tax. Part of the sale pitch of the GST was that it would leave a paper trail, making it much more difficult for people to cheat on their taxes.
But when Finance Minister Don Mazankowski delivered his budget last month, the numbers indicated GST revenue was $1.2 billion less than projected in February 1991. The government blames the recession for the shortfall.
May 10, 1993

Canadians are fed up with the government, fed up with its approach, fed up with the way it keeps the books and cooks them sometimes, fed up-
Oh, oh.
Yes, yes, I will repeat it: cooks them sometimes.
Oh, oh.

It is not oh, oh; it is the truth. Last year the Auditor General for the first time had three reservations on the government dealing with the way it dealt with pensions, with the federal-provincial payments and the Petro-Canada deal. It had three reservations. It was a record of complaints by the Auditor General against the incumbent government.
This government should be booted out, not only for its incompetence but for its cuteness in trying to make Canadians believe this year's change of the rebate in January does not mean very much. It just going to be included in April. It has decreased its deficit next year by some $625 million and that should be repeated to Canadians. They are a bunch of incompetents.

Mr. Speaker, again we listen to the blustering from the Liberals. When they do not have a good point we notice the volume of their voices goes up. They yell, rant and rave about mismanagement and so on and so forth.
My hon. friend still did not answer my very direct question whether the Standing Committee on Finance found that the GST was the fairest tax. I might remind the hon. member that these amendments are being brought in to help small business with the GST. I might also remind him it is the largest tax change the country has seen since the Liberals brought income tax in on a temporary basis.
The Liberals brought income tax into this country on a temporary basis just to pay for the First World War. Then they were to wipe it out and we have had it ever since. I mean their track record on taxes is not that great either.
I want to ask the hon. member this direct question. I want him to answer me. If the Standing Committee on Finance finds that the goods and services tax is the proper tax and the fairest tax we can have on a value
Government Orders
added basis, will the Liberals then back off on their promise to wipe out the goods and services tax and replace it with something "we are not sure of yet but Canadian people trust us because we Liberals can really be trusted"?

Mr. Speaker, the only reason I raise my voice is because when the transport minister and the minister of privatization both yell at the same time it is difficult to be heard in this place. I want the microphone to hear me and not them. That is the reason I have to raise my voice sometimes.
The minister has asked me a hypothetical question. I have only been here 20 years but my experience taught me something some time ago. A former leader of my party, Mr. Trudeau, who was a good Prime Minister said hypothetical questions should be compared with the following analogy: If my grandmother had wheels we would call her a bus. It does not make any sense to answer a hypothetical question. If the spirit of today prevails across the land Canadians will throw out the government and the GST. I will bet the minister a private lunch that if a committee travels across the country it will come back and say to get rid of the GST.

Mr. Speaker, I just wanted to compliment the member for Ottawa-Vanier on an excellent address. He noted the key problems.
I know government members keep asking us what we will replace the GST with. We have been telling them all along that it is very simple. We are going to consult Canadians rather than ram it down their throats the way the government has done over the last number of years.
I wonder whether the member for Ottawa-Vanier would like to talk about the fact the information that came out of the committee hearings is that the GST generated revenue of $30 billion but only netted $15 billion to the Treasury. When we look at those numbers and see the amount of money going out in rebates, administration costs and all those things, we have to start rethinking this tax. It clearly shows that it does not work.

Mr. Speaker, these are excellent questions. The Public Accounts of Canada show that Canadians contributed $29.45 billion to the GST in 1991-92. After rebates and credits the net was $15.2 billion. I do not know of any ship or railway that operates without administration. Salaries have to be paid. There is rent, equipment and supplies. After deducting $486 million

May 10, 1993
Government Orders
for administration $14.5 billion is left. We collected $29.5 billion. This is very inefficient.
No, no.

I hear the minister saying no, no. I dare him to find in the Public Accounts of Canada anything different. I happen to know those figures by heart. I am not twisting anything. I am giving the truth. That is the
government's game.
I dare the minister to contradict my figures right now. The GST is a 50 per cent efficient tax. It is absolutely no good. It is inefficient and heavy. In one simple word it is bad.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to join this debate as well on Bill C-112, an act to amend the Excise Tax Act, the Access to Information Act, the Canada Pension Plan, the Customs Act, the Federal Court Act, the Income 'lax Act, the Tax Court of Canada Act, the Thx Rebate Discounting Act, the Unemployment Insurance Act and a related act.
After just reading the title it is really a bill filled with complexities and one that will need thorough study. For the government to introduce the concept of secrecy in part of the bill certainly raises immediate concerns in the eyes of many Canadians.
I would like to focus my debate on three points: the specific concerns about the bill itself, some of the evils of the GST and perhaps a word about deficit reduction strategy.
First on the bill itself, I would like to indicate that the absence of a level playing field for the co-operatives to operate within this proposed Bill C-112 certainly is unfair to the co-operatives in the country. Why this government is allowing it to happen remains difficult for me to understand. Why an amendment by the Liberal Party to correct this obvious deficiency was not accepted by this government to me only reflects the continuing insensitivity of this government to co-operatives in the country.
Second, the cloak of secrecy that can insulate vital economic and monetary information and data from closer scrutiny by the Canadian public certainly is a
weakness in this bill because it is a truism that information is critical when we ask Canadians to participate in the democratic processes and to allow them to participate meaningfully and to criticize the policies of this government.
When one hears that this government is introducing the cloak of secrecy and the barrier to access to information by the Canadian public one can only sort of guess that the government is afraid to be fully scrutinized by Canadians.
There is the complexity of the bill itself. It is known that the backbone of the economy of this country rests with small businesses. Small businesses have felt that the GST is a very complex tax measure and yet here is again a bill thousands of pages long that they have to read through again. Even the provision on retroactivity to 1991 definitely would be very harmful. Again that relates to the insensitivity of this government.
If we have a bill like this that would need a team of lawyers and tax consultants to help businesses then obviously the cost to businesses will increase. What will happen to the owners of the corner-stores around the country? What will happen to them? I ask this government to reflect on the financial burden that will be imposed upon them.
I would say again that with respect to the retroactivity provision that certainly it is becoming a habit of this government to always have a retroactive provision as it did with the bill on the pharmaceuticals.
There is the GST and how small businesses and the economy are harmed. My colleagues have already articulated during debate that following the accumulation of some $30 billion in revenue, the end result is a net of about $15 billion in revenue. To have 50 cents of every dollar collected as the net revenue for the country truly does not speak well of the efficiency of the system. This government prides itself that this is one of its strengths but this certainly is a serious indictment of its claim.
Second, the GST has not enhanced at all federal and provincial relations. At the same time the GST has not helped reduce the national financial deficit. No wonder this tax has been the most hated one in the country.
May 10, 1993

During debate I heard one spokesperson for the NDP indicate that there is no single tax measure that could replace the GST. I agree with that. Yet what we heard in debate from that NDP spokesperson is only one small component of the package he is trying to sell.
I would like to make a simple comparison of this bill for Canadians in so far as the stand of this Tory government, of the NDP and of the Liberal Party. First, it is clear that a Tory government will continue the GST. It is a commitment on its part. I would call it stubbornness on its part despite the obvious harm that it has created for Canadian businesses and many Canadian consumers.
In contrast the New Democratic Party has indicated through its leader that it will phase it out over five years. The maximum term of any government under our Constitution is five years. In fact by tradition the election has to be called within four years.
This Tory government has already exceeded that parliamentary tradition and the election should have been called already. Yet the New Democratic Party is telling Canadians that it would phase out the GST in five years, in other words beyond the usual traditional life of a Parliament.
If the GST is as bad as the NDP claims and as we believe it is in the Liberal Party then why should it take the NDP five years? Imagine a patient with cancer and one says that it is a serious disease: "Oh, but it will take me five years to apply all my treatment approaches". That is not the way to treat a malignant and serious problem. That is not the way to treat a malignant and serious public policy issue in the country.
The Liberal Party, in contrast, is committed to changing and abolishing the GST within 12 months. During that time, we would consult with Canadians again contrasting with the other party that would not even like to consult with Canadians or the provinces. It would not like to consult with the provinces. It is inherent in taxation that we should have the full consent of the governed, including that of the provincial governments.
I have a word about deficit reduction strategy and about fiscal responsibility. The Tory government would
Government Orders
like deficit reduction at all cost with cuts to all programs.
I would like to submit that the Liberal Party is equally committed to deficit reduction but with an approach with a social conscience and a Canadian sense of values.
What do I mean by that? We are committed to maintaining funding appropriately for health care, education and employment strategy. We want to help those severely dislocated from their jobs with the unemployment insurance social safety net.
I would like to add that one approach to fiscal responsibility is this aspect of government streamlining. How many departments of government are there today that duplicate their efforts and therefore the cost to the Canadian taxpayers. One can only imagine one issue that I addressed earlier in this Chamber. That is the provision for example of immigrant and settlement services.
The employment department of this country, the immigration department as well as the Department of Multiculturalism are involved in this process. Why is it not one department of government? This is only one glaring example of government administrative inefficiency that we can attack and thereby save tax money for the Canadian taxpayers.
Last, I would like to indicate that in terms of an approach to governance we have to instil and re-instil in our governments the principle of public ethics and trust. No more shall there be contracts that the Auditor General will tell us report after report have been granted by government presumably illegally.
I can recall some 20 contracts given by the health department that were under RCMP investigation. We have yet to see the report by the RCMP on this issue. I would like the government to table this report as soon as it is out. That is where we could save money. There are other sources of revenue. We could maximize the utilization of revenues that are collected.
I am really delighted to speak briefly on this bill during debate and to indicate to the House that this bill as it is now contains flaws and ought to be rectified. I challenge the government to do so and listen to the Liberal view. As well we would like to just reiterate to this Chamber that the Liberal Party is committed to abolish the GST,

May 10, 1993
Government Orders
not over five years as the NDP would like us to believe, but truly within the first year of government.

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I congratulate you on your promotion to such a lofty position.
We heard it again that the Liberals are going to wipe out the goods and services tax and replace it within one year.
In 1986 the government of the day, after listening to the recommendations of royal commissions and standing committees in this House, decided to take away a very detrimental manufacturers' sales tax which everybody agreed was a bad tax. That recommendation had been around for 40 years. The Conservatives were the first ones to move on it.
Why did you raise it to 13 per cent then?
It was a bad tax.
That's right and that is why it was a bad tax. It was a terrible tax. We raised it. Absolutely we raised it.
Three times.

That is right. The government did raise it three times. It was a bad tax. We said that and we said that we were going to replace it. We said it in 1986. At that time there were three options presented to the Canadian people. There were countless hearings across the country on the goods and services tax. The government chose the type of tax system that we have here after consultation with Canadians between 1986 and 1988 when we made our decision.
Then in 1988 we had an election. At that time the Canadian people knew that the Conservative government was bringing in a goods and services tax.
Did you hear what the member for Mississauga South said?

I campaigned on it. I remember the Minister of Finance at the time making a commitment that there would be no additional taxes on new housing and that it would be the same as the manufacturers' sales tax. I also remember making a commitment that there would be no taxes on food at the time. I remember saying
that during the campaign. We campaigned on it. Ib say that we did not campaign on it is entirely erroneous.
I want to ask my hon. friend his opinion. He says that he is going to replace the sales tax within a year and replace it with something. We are not sure what yet but the Liberals are asking the Canadian people to trust them: "We will bring you something different that is going to raise the same amount of revenue but we do not know what it is yet. We are going to eliminate this tax and we are going to do it within a year".
I am going to ask him again. If he goes across this country and finds out that there are no alternatives but that they remain with the goods and services tax, will the Liberals stick with the goods and services tax if that is what the standing committee on finance finds?

Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to respond to the comments and questions posed by the hon. minister.
It is certainly true that this government consulted with the finance committee and with Canadians. It is true and I should give the government credit about that. However, there is a fundamental difference between hearing and listening. When this government heard the concerns of Canadians the vast majority of Canadians-85 per cent-were opposed to the GST but it insisted stubbornly to introduce the tax. Therefore this government did not listen to the wishes of Canadians.
We are more confident of the intelligence of the ordinary Canadian. When we consult with them I am confident that we will hear a proposal that is sensitive, simple, efficient and effective. When we hear that we will have the new tax approach to this country that is fair for all. Because I am confident of Canadians I decline, with all respect, to answer a hypothetical question that is premised on a faulty basis and that is that Canadians will tell us that they like the GST. It is not a fact. The truth is that Canadians do not like the GST. Therefore to even answer the question, which is hypothetical, will be insulting to many Canadians and prejudging that consultation process.

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

Give the rest of us a chance, John.
May 10, 1993
The hon. member is in caucus with him and can ask him these questions in caucus. I do not have that chance.
He has made some good points.

Then let me give him an opportunity to make some more. How is that, okay?
I want to ask my hon. friend this question that is not hypothetical but a direct question that I am sure he can answer. If the Liberals are going into a campaign with this campaign promise on the goods and services tax and they are going to consult with the Canadian people then might I ask my friend why the Liberals have not consulted with the people before the election?.
We are.

Why have the Liberals not come up with a concrete proposal so that during the election they will in fact have something to compare it to rather than a pig in a poke? That is like saying: "Trust us. We will wipe out in a year and we will bring something else in that you want". Why do they not consult the Canadian people now and give us a concrete proposal as their alternative to the goods and services tax?
Mr. Speaker, Canadians have told us and have told this government that they do not like the GST. So we have made a definitive conclusion that we will abolish the GST.
What are you going to replace it with? Income tax?

The second piart of the question, which he really did not make clear, is what specific proposals we will introduce. The minister is telling us that we will have a document very high in technicalities and that we will run it through during the election debate. That is not the way to consult with Canadians. That is not the way to consult with the provinces. This government is so stubborn about the GST that it is not even willing to listen to common sense logic.

Mr. Speaker, I heard the hon. member say that he trusts the intelligence of Canadians. I think that the Liberals had better fear the intelligence of Canadians. We just heard a sudden, late moment development from the hon.
Government Orders
member. The Liberals are going to abolish the GST. I just do not know what their means of communication might be but I wonder if that word has gone to their leader who seems to be far behind this hon. member. He does not know what they are going to do.
I heard the hon. member's analogy about the New Democrats where he said that the GST is going to be phased out over five years: "What ill patient would want to wait that long?" I wonder how many ill patients are going to have their diseases treated by committee. This is an absurdity.
My simple question is this. I would like to see the coherent tax policy document that commits the Liberals to the abolition of the GST and which will provide the basis on which this committee will discuss the issue of taxation with Canadians and arrive at its conclusion. Where is the specific declaration that there will be no GST or value-added tax imposed upon Canadians by the Liberals? A clear concrete answer will do and then maybe the intelligence of the Canadian people can be trusted rather than feared.

Mr. Speaker, the member indicated that the Liberals have not made a specific declaration. I would truly refer the hon. member to all the clippings in the country and to all the television clips that are there. He should research the Library of Parliament and he will see very clearly that the Liberals have made a specific declaration and commitment to abolish the GST. That way of perpetuating falsehoods has to be put to rest.
Your leader had better catch up with the rest of you then.
The NDP prides itself in consulting with Canadians and now is telling us that it would not like to consult them any more. I leave that judgment to Canadians out there in the country.

Mr. Speaker, the temptation is great to explore further this fascinating new concept of mandate that the Liberal Party of Canada is proposing to carry into the next election. I hope in fact before my remarks are concluded that I might have the opportunity to come back to this. Again, I

May 10,1993
Government Orders
must say that this is a fascinating new concept of mandate.
You have 20 minutes. Tell us about you. Tell us about what you will do.

Let me instead turn to some matters more substantively dealt with in the bill before us. I refer specifically to the provisions of the bill as they will impact on the co-op sector in Canada.
I am a member of a the Delton Co-Operative Association Ltd. I have been member number 152618 for several years and intend to remain so for as long as I draw breath. I am a big supporter of co-ops because they perform many worth-while functions in the communities in which they do business, not least of which is keeping the profits from their operations, when there are profits, within those communities.
Canada's co-ops do not shift billions of dollars a year out of our economy. They keep the money within the economy and in the community to help it grow and meet its own needs. That is very valuable. Any prudent government would do what it could to ensure that co-ops have every possible benefit in their work.
Unfortunately the bill before us provides the exact opposite. Current GST regulations put retail co-ops at a competitive disadvantage vis-a-vis their vertically integrated corporate competitors because the tiered structure of co-op wholesale and ownership functions is such that at each step of the way within the co-op network the GST must be passed through. I will start again for example in my own home co-op with materials purchased or manufactured by Federated Co-operatives out of Saskatchewan and then marketed to my local co-op, Delton Co-Operative Association Ltd.
The government does not derive any revenue from this exercise. The passing through of GST costs within the co-op structure generates not a single penny for the federal government in net GST revenue. It does increase vastly the administrative costs incurred by the co-ops.
This is not the case for the vertically integrated private sector major retail chains which perform all of these functions within one corporate entity. They do not have those administrative overheads at each step of the retail process that the co-ops do. These overhead costs for
co-ops amount to hundreds of thousands of dollars, for example, in the Atlantic region alone. I know that in western Canada, in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, that figure would run quite probably into the millions of dollars. Co-ops are a huge concern in western Canada. This cost to the co-ops and only to the co-ops generates not a penny for the federal government.
The GST structure also discriminates against so-called direct charge retail co-ops, which charge weekly operating fees to members. Some of these are sometimes as well called pre-buy co-ops. This fee covers both the overhead of the store and the members' equity in the co-operative.
Remember, no GST is charged on any other form of investment. The government has recognized the fact that this GST charge on member's equity and direct charge co-ops is inequitable and ought not to be there.
This was recognized as early as June 1991 when it removed the GST charged on other forms of co-operative equity, but that charge still remains on the member's equity in direct charge retail co-ops. The government thus far has been unwilling to treat direct charge equity fairly.
Direct charge co-ops are a significant and growing concern in Canada with large numbers located in Atlantic Canada and British Columbia.
There is a direct charge co-op in Yellowknife which at times has a two-year waiting list. That is the measure of the popularity of that direct charge co-op in Yellowknife, and it is not uncharacteristic. This is a very popular way for Canadians to do business because it is a relatively inexpensive way and the profits, the surpluses generated by this economic activity, remain in the communities where the activity is undertaken.
Co-ops provide an alternative for communities, especially places like Yellowknife, elsewhere in the isolated north, remote and lower income communities, that would otherwise be at the mercy of monopoly grocery chains.
Consumer co-ops in Canada have an awful lot of members. There are 1,655,000 co-op members in Canada.
May 10, 1993

In total, co-ops do a volume of business of over $3.2 billion a year and employ 16,000 people across the country. Co-ops are a crucial part of the Canadian economy, both in rural and urban areas. That is why New Democrats not only recognize that co-ops are a vital ingredient in the Canadian economy but in our strategy for a full employment economy we propose to foster the further development of co-ops.
This policy includes a firm commitment to the equality of treatment for co-operatives by the federal government which means, among other considerations, that the GST currently charged on administrative transactions within the co-op structure should be eliminated. It is one of the major flaws of the bill before us that this is not done.
Unfortunately it would seem that at this third reading stage that flaw will remain. It is unfortunate because there is no fiscal reason for the federal government to maintain that charge and the economic arguments against it are significant.
The co-op movement in Canada is one of the potential bright spots in what is otherwise still, as it has been for several years now, a fairly bleak picture.
Co-ops in Canada have the capacity to serve virtually all consumer needs where they are located and they have the potential to constitute an entirely new form of productive economic enterprise in this country: enterprises owned by the people who work in them and who rely on them for goods and services, that are dedicated to the communities in which they are located, and that in the long run hold far greater potential for good in this country than does the standard, classic, free enterprise, privately owned model.
That being the case, any prudent government would be vitally interested in fostering the well-being of co-ops. This bill does not do that. It works against the well-being of co-ops and on those grounds alone ought to be defeated. I see that our time has run into Question Period so I will resume later.
It being two o'clock p.m., the House will now proceed to statements by members pursuant to Standing Order 31.

Mr. Speaker, members of the Association des prospecteurs du Quebec and I have been trying to convince federal officials and the Minister of Finance to help the recovery of mining exploration in Canada through low-cost tax measures.
We have made representations to officials at the Department of Finance and the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources.
The deputy ministers are not interested in our resource regions and do not understand the situation in the mining exploration sector in Abitibi.

Mr. Speaker, the fate of language minorities often rests with the provinces. We know the problems caused by Bill 178 in Quebec, which restricted the right to bilingual signage. We also know how provinces with an anglophone majority reacted to this bill.
Quebec's Bill 178 has often been used by the other provinces as an excuse to suppress the basic rights of francophone minorities. The Quebec government has taken a major step toward eliminating an irritant that is unfair to its own language minority and has now allowed bilingual signage in Quebec.
It is high time provinces with an anglophone majority, including Ontario, my own province, were as positive in their treatment of their francophone minorities. Whether we are talking about constitutional rights, school management or the survival of minorities, Canada must survive.

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of barley producers in the riding of Macleod I call upon the government to implement the dual continental barley market proposal.

May 10, 1993
A dual continental market offers our producers the freedom to choose, to market their product either independently and privately or through the Canadian Wheat Board. This small measure would help liberate the most productive, efficient and effective farmers in the world.
Canada is only a small player in the U.S. feed grain market. Our barley exports into the U.S. represent only 1.25 per cent of the Canadian Wheat Board's total sales, yet there would be gains in a continental barley market.
This injection of cash into the pockets of hard-working barley producers will reduce the need for taxpayer support and continue to promote self-reliance.
A dual continental market is one more step in helping our producers get the returns from the market and not from the taxpayer. I urge the government to endorse this concept.

Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate Gordon McIntyre of Huntingdon, Quebec for his successful battle to protect his language rights. It was Mr. McIntyre's case which went to the UN human rights committee and which resulted in its April ruling that Quebec's sign law was a denial of freedom. I am pleased to say that I have supported Mr. McIntyre's case since 1989.
As a result of the UN ruling and other political action the Quebec government has now introduced Bill 86 to allow English on commercial signs and relax other restrictions. While this is not a perfect bill it is a definite step forward in recognizing minority language rights and will help resolve similar issues throughout the country.
While I fully support measures to protect and enhance the French language in Canada this can and must be done without suppressing English.
We are fortunate to have French and English as our official languages and we should rejoice in the opportunity to use both to our political and economic advantage in Canada and throughout the world.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to bring to the attention of the Minister of Employment and Immigration and the general public the generous actions of the staff at the Amherst Canada Employment Centre.
When a fellow member of the CEC, Mrs. Margaret McMaster, was diagnosed with a serious illness requiring a heart-lung transplant her fellow workers responded immediately by establishing a fund raising campaign to help her with the tremendous costs of the operation. By working nights and weekends the entire staff and management, led by claims clerk Dan Hill, have raised close to $10,000 through car washes, bake sales, casino nights and a major raffle. As well, they contacted other CEC offices and the business community and have had excellent results.
The staff at Amherst CEC deserve a tremendous amount of credit for their outstanding effort to aid one of their co-workers. It is also quite a compliment to Mrs. McMaster that her colleagues would come to her assistance in such a meaningful way. Then again, Mr. Speaker, if you knew Margaret McMaster you would understand their eagerness to help.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to bring the attention of the House to the plight of one of the world's greatest treasures, our marine wildlife.
Today in Japan some members of the International Whaling Commission are fighting hard to maintain the commission's 10-year moratorium on the commercial killing of whales. These countries understand the precarious position of our threatened whale populations and at least want more time for scientific research into the seriousness of the problem.
France is lobbying for a whale sanctuary in the Antarctic south of 40 degrees latitude. Such a sanctuary could begin the process of conserving one of the world's most amazing but misunderstood species.
The actions of countries like Norway and Japan contradict all those seemingly sincere commitments made at the earth summit in Rio last year. Canada
May 10, 1993

should bring its influence to bear on these countries and demonstrate its support for both a continued moratorium on commercial whaling and the creation of a whale sanctuary south of the 40.

Mr. Speaker, in February I sent surveys to all the households in my riding. The purpose of this exercise was to get feedback about the issues Canadians face each day. Here are a few things some constituents said on the subject of MPs and their role in the House of Commons. One comment was:
An MP should be aware of the opinions of constituents but also should be aware of the global results of any decisions. In other words, they should be much more informed than the general populace. Then they are in a position to make valid decisions.
Another comment was:
Clean up the way business is handled in the House of Commons. The current in-house bickering is an embarrassment to all Canadians.
Another comment:
Thke time to stand back from the established norm. Identify with the locals, not with fellow politicians.
A final one was:
MPs are elected to exercise leadership and judgment and not to take a narrow view.
These are just a few of the hundreds of comments that were made. We have a very serious responsibility here in the House of Commons. I am honoured to be here and to serve my constituents in Edmonton-Strathcona.
