Mr. Speaker, I am outraged by reports that the Heritage Front, an extremist right wing organization which sees itself as an umbrella organization for a host of smaller white supremacist groups, including Ku Klux Klan cells and skinhead gangs, has indicated its intention to commence an active recruitment process in the Ottawa area. Residents of the nation's capital have declared that it is not welcome here.
The Heritage Front reflects a disturbing trend in Canadian society. This past year has seen a significant increase in both hate crimes and hate propaganda. Some of the most vile and repulsive hate propaganda imaginable is now flooding into Canada, and in some cases being produced in Canada, in far greater volume than at any time in the recent past.
I commend the more than 100 anti-racist high school students who recently strode through downtown Ottawa to add their voices to fight against racism. The time has come for all of us to step up the battle against racism in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, my riding of Wild Rose is in the heart of barley growing country in Alberta.
Over the past few days, I have received faxes and phone calls from literally hundreds of farmers. Their message to me is simple. They want a choice in the way they market their own barley to the United States.
These producers say there are significant opportunities for barley sales to the U.S., opportunities that producers themselves are better able to access than the Canadian Wheat Board. With these opportunities will come higher returns for their crops.
At a time of low farm incomes the government should support any measure which will mean higher revenue for farmers. I urge the minister and the government to move quickly on this issue and to give fanners a choice.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday marked the first anniversary of the Westray mine disaster which claimed the lives of 26 coal miners in Nova Scotia.
I wish to extend my sincere sympathies to the families of the victims who have had to endure not only the pain and suffering from losing a loved one but also the bewilderment and frustration of having many important questions remain unanswered.

May 10, 1993
Tragedy can be defined in many ways and has been used to describe many terrible events. Am entire community was devastated. A community of good, hard-working and honest people was literally crushed by an occurrence beyond its control.
Words can never fully express the magnitude of the disaster that befell the Westray coal mine on that day. They seem inadequate for the task but words, at the end of the day, are all that we have.
With words we pledge to work tirelessly as long as it takes to find justice for those families and truth for all.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Saturday I attended a public meeting hosted by the South West Nova Long Line Fishermen's Association. These fishermen are gravely concerned about how they are going to pay their bills when the 4X haddock quota expires.
Some people do not have a lot of sympathy for fishermen who in good years have been known to make a very handsome living. However, no matter how much money a fisherman takes in it is only meaningful in the context of how much it costs to maintain his operation, a situation that is not unlike that of a highly capitalized prairie farm. With or without quota, boat payments, wharfage charges, equipment costs and other expenses must be met.
If the government wishes to avoid large numbers of bankruptcies among our fishermen this year then either the means must be found to provide financial support to Nova Scotia's fishermen in southern and western Nova Scotia or else the means must be found to keep them fishing.

Mr. Speaker, once again we have Liberals making promises, this time to the agricultural community.
Promises of income stabilization come from a Liberal Party which when in government never followed through
when it had the opportunity to bring forward a comprehensive income stabilization program.
Promises of a national food security plan come from a Liberal Party which when in government supported an interest rate policy which forced hundreds of farmers into bankruptcy and off the land, which when in government introduced rail line abandonment across the country.
Promises of assurance that food production is seen as an important sovereignty issue come from a Liberal Party which has failed to tell Canadians what it would do in response to the catastrophe of the free trade agreement and now the North American free trade deal.
The Liberal agriculture policy is one to be funded by cutting other programs without telling Canadians the precise program cuts to be made. Liberals cannot continue making announcements about what they will do for Canadians in the expectation that Canadians will forget what Liberal governments have done to Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to decry the last minute appeal by the cities of Detroit and Windsor to block the construction of the proposed CN rail tunnel between Sarnia, Ontario and Port Huron, Michigan.
The proposed tunnel will accommodate doublestacked trains that cannot travel through the existing tunnels. It will help CN become more competitive and deliver more traffic more efficiency.
In particular I regret that the mayor of Windsor has seen fit to join in the desperate effort to block a project that is so vital to the future and the economic development of our community of Sarnia-Lambton. This $150 million investment will have considerable spin-offs for our entire area. One vital fact that these two mayors seem to have forgotten is that if CN cannot build this tunnel under the St. Clair River, it will not substitute one under the Detroit River between Detroit and Windsor.
In a highly competitive North American freight business it is regrettable that political posturing and self-interest is muddying the waters for an important business
May 10, 1993

Oral Questions
decision made by CN which has been based upon economic and environmental considerations.

Mr. Speaker, a picture is worth a thousand words.
Thke the wonderful photo of the two once wild, now deceased boars, Boris Yeltsin and our very own Prime Minister. There he is grinning from ear to ear, extremely pleased by his latest coup on the international scene. Why should he not be pleased?
Then the photo showed up in Canadian newspapers and the Prime Minister stopped smiling, or so we are told, but why? Why should Canadians not have the satisfaction of knowing that our very own Prime Minister is getting full value out of the million dollars we are spending on his hunting trip. Surely the man who brought us the GST, the free trade agreement and record unemployment deserves that much. Canadians are a grateful people.
A picture is worth a thousand words, sometimes even more.

Mr. Speaker, on April 30 this year, in the presence of Bill Caine of Commonwealth Plywood, Mayor Carmelle Nantel and members of the community, I turned the first sod in Belleterre to signal the start of construction on a sawmill to replace the mill which burnt down in 1989.
This project, worth $7 million, will create 70 new jobs in Belleterre and help maintain 35 jobs at the veneer plant.
I am very pleased with the contribution by the federal office of regional development for Quebec, because without that contribution of more than $1,400,000, the project would never have materialized.
This is good news for a community that has suffered severe setbacks in recent years. I say three cheers for the people of Belleterre and good luck to the present and future workers at the sawmill.

Mr. Speaker, we were not surprised when the free trade agreement failed the Canadian steel industry. We were not surprised when the U.S. rejected our blue ribbon panel which suggested a sectoral agreement. But we were surprised when our own Canadian International Trade Tribunal decided that other countries are dumping steel plate into our market but the Americans are not.
This ruling was rendered despite Revenue Canada's preliminary decision to apply duties in all of the countries including the United States.
How can we accept rulings that allow the Americans to apply a 69 per cent duty on our exports and we apply zero per cent to their imports into our market? I guess one of the hidden conditions of free trade is that the Americans have total access to our market and we are shut out of theirs.
This trade war will benefit neither side, but if we are to fight the battle on a level playing field we require new generals, new strategies, and some armaments such as a trade law with some teeth with which to fight.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Acting Prime Minister. While the Prime Minister was away on a fabulous hunting and fishing expedition in Russia, in Canada the unemployment rate rose to 11.4 per cent. This increase was not caused by the fact that more people were looking for work, and Statistics Canada made it clear that it was because of the number of people who lost their jobs last month.
If this government's economic policies are so good, why are Canadian workers still losing their jobs in this country?

May 10, 1993
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we did not take any delight whatsoever in the employment statistics that came out on Friday.
I remind the hon. Leader of Her Majesty's Official Opposition that one month of statistics does not a trend make. If he looks at what has happened over the last 12 months he will see there has been an increase in employment in 10 of the last 12 months. As a matter of fact 151,000 full-time jobs have been created in that period of time. In April the manufacturing jobs which the opposition is always harping about increased by 28,000. That is a gain of 70,000 since last October.
There are some good signs in the economy and employment in certain sectors is improving. We believe as the economy improves so will the job prospects for Canadians.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
In the
month of April we lost 43,000 jobs, more than 1,400 a day. For the minister to get up and say that the situation is improving is very difficult for unemployed Canadians to accept.
The Prime Minister is off hunting in Russia, but when will he stop targeting wild boar and start targeting the Canadian economy and creating jobs for Canadians?

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speechtext:
Speaking of bores, Mr. Speaker, there are good signs in the economy which the leader of the Liberal Party never points out.
He never talks about the increase in the growth of the economy, the gross domestic product growing over the last quarter by 3.5 per cent. Today we saw a dramatic increase in housing starts of some 22,000 bringing the annualized rate to some 170,000. I might add this was in April, a month when builders told me they had to hold back somewhat because of the weather conditions. There are lots of good signs out there.
Day after day the hon. leader gets up in the House and says how terrible things are in Canada which really does not do much to promote confidence in this country. He should have more confidence in Canada. He should stand up here and praise Canada not denigrate-
The hon. Leader of the Opposition.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is very difficult to talk about good things with this government. The average Canadian's income in constant dollars was better when this government came into power than after nine years of Tory administration. Not only that, when his colleague, the Minister of Finance, introduced his budget a few days ago he said that this year and next there would still be more than 11 per cent unemployment in Canada.
When will the government wake up to reality and start creating real jobs for Canadians who would love nothing better than to work?

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, that is exactly what the government is doing. It is allowing the private sector to create real jobs. It is not throwing money at problems like the Leader of the Opposition wants to do in make-work projects and temporary jobs for about 30,000 people. That is not the way to solve the problem. The way to solve it is to get the basics in place and allow the private sector to create the jobs. That is what is going to happen with our policies.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Acting Prime Minister.
The number of unemployed workers in Quebec rose by 16,000 last month. This means that daily, 533 workers lost their jobs, every day for 30 days. Why did the minister refuse to include a job creation program in its last budget that would put one-half million unemployed workers in Quebec back to work and put a stop to the pauperization of Canadians?

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that is coming from the party that voted against every single proposal brought forward by this government to help the province of Quebec, including research and development in the drug industry. That has been very important to the economic increases in Montreal.
The hon. member might also be interested in reading the reports from the IMF, the OECD and some of the financial organizations which are saying that the eco-
May 10, 1993

nomic growth in Quebec is going to be the best of all of the provinces in Canada this year.
We have put the basics in place. It is going to happen. The hon. member will not be happy when it has happened because he will have nothing to complain about.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if the government's proposal is as good as the minister says it is, why is Montreal now the poverty capital of this country? Why have families lost an average of $2,000 since this government came to power?
Since the last nine budgets have created a disastrous situation, will this government, as it nears the end of its term, at least and at last introduce a concrete proposal for creating jobs and give Canadians new hope?

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the only proposal the Liberals have brought forward is to throw money at make-work projects on a short-term basis. That is the only proposal they have.
With respect to the other two proposals recommended by the Canadian Association of Realtors and the Canadian Home Builders' Association, this government implemented them and it is paying dividends today.
I want to ask the hon. member whether he thinks his make-work project is going to create the required number of jobs in Quebec. The answer of course is no. It is a phoney make-work project that lasts for a very short period of time.
What we want is for the private sector to create full-time meaningful employment, exactly what we saw last month when 28,000 jobs were created in the manufacturing industry. Real full-time jobs. That is what we want.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the minister of health.
Oral Questions
When the minister announced that he was leaving public life he said he would support no candidate for the Conservative leadership, but added that he would leap in if he saw any of them challenging our social safety net. Since that time we have had direct challenges to universal health care through proposals for user fees made by both the Minister of National Defence and the Minister of the Environment.
I want to ask the minister of health whether he stands by the principles of the Canada Health Act which penalizes user fees. Will he repudiate the proposals to allow user fees made by his fellow cabinet ministers?

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have always said that I stand by the principles of the health care system. I repeat that again today.
However, I am amazed that members of the House are worried about the questioning of this country's social policies. The provinces of Newfoundland, Quebec and Alberta have all raised the question of user fees. They did this in the perspective that the future of this country's social policies have to be considered today.
The questions are a reflection of the social policies. It does not mean user fees will be implemented tomorrow. It is a straight responsibility by a government. It is what my colleagues, the Minister of National Defence and the Minister of the Environment, referred to. They did not say that they would implement user fees. They said that they would re-examine the social policy. We heard that day after day from the opposition. I wonder why when it is done by the government, which is once again a responsible action, it is seen as unacceptable.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary is for the same minister. The primary reason we are having this controversy over user fees is that the provinces have seen a swift decline in the federal share of medicare funding from almost 50 per cent in 1979 to 33 per cent in 1993 to a projected 23 per cent by the year 2000. The provinces do not endorse these unilateral cuts. As Glen Clark, the B.C. minister of finance, has said: "Shifting financial burdens on the provinces is inappropriate and counterproductive".

May 10, 1993
Oral Questions
Will the minister deal with the financial squeeze that is promoting user fees by lifting the five-year freeze on health care financing?

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope that the B.C. minister of finance has consulted the minister of health and welfare who has said publicly that there was enough money in the system. It is not a question of pulling the 5 per cent cap on the transfer to the provinces.
Many times the hon. member has made wrong affirmations in this House. He is wrong when he said that we froze the increase of support to the provinces on the health care system. That increase has been constant since 1984 and will continue to be. Members of the NDP as usual say to put money, put money and put money. They should consult the provinces of Saskatchewan, B.C. and Ontario. They will tell them exactly what they want to do, cut their spending maybe because of what they said in Ontario recently.

My supplementary is for the same minister.
There are warning signs everywhere that the health of medicare is going downhill with the proposals for private clinics, private hospitals and user fees. Soon we will no longer have a Canadian health care system. Instead we will have 12 separate U.S.-style systems.
Will the minister take this opportunity to say no to user fees and no to any Conservative leadership candidate who is seeking to bring a U.S.-style health care system to Canada?
Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of National Health
and Welfare): Mr. Speaker, as usual, this is fear-monger-ing by the NDP. The hon. member is talking about user fees, private clinics and so on. He knows veiy well that the system in Canada has to be one of public management. That is within the law. He knows that very well. Once again he puts out strong ideas publicly and thinks that people will believe them.
It is normal that Canadians raise questions about the health care system and social policies today as has always been done in many countries in the world. The fact of the matter is that for nine years this government has respected the principle of the health care system. I have listened to what the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance said last week and I am repeating that today.
The principles are there. The government is committed to that and there is no reason to believe we will change that policy.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister for International Trade.
Thousands of jobs in Canada's steel industry have been put at risk by a recent decision made by the Canadian International Trade Tribunal. The problem is that when Americans export to Canada they do so under conditions that are far more advantageous than the conditions Canadians face when they export to the United States.
Why didn't this government act before the dispute, to make our rules as strict as those imposed by the Americans? Mr. Speaker, Canadians want to export steel, not jobs.

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International TYade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, by and large the trade remedy laws of the United States and Canada are very much the same. There is very little difference between them. Timing is one difference, the timing for changes to be made. There are some changes in the finer points of how the trade remedy laws are implemented.
I appreciate the concern my hon. friend is raising. It is a concern we have on the government side as well, but it is something we are looking at in view of the decision the CITT has taken recently. I appreciate my hon. friend's interest in it.

Mr. Speaker, only a puppet government whose strings were pulled in Washington could think that we are talking about the finer points. This is a hole you can drive a truck through.
Thousands of jobs in the Canadian steel industry are at stake and the reason is very clear. It is because after the free trade agreement, the government failed to make our trade rules as tough as those of the Americans.
May 10, 1993

Will the government commit now to changing our trade rules on dumping and injury so that, first, the U.S. faces the same burden of proof when it exports to Canada as we do when we export to the United States?
Second, will the government ensure that if the United States will not exempt Canada from the scope of its world-wide trading actions, then we will not exempt it when it comes here?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International TVade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I suggest my hon. friend stick to questions on the environment because he is demonstrating his lack of knowledge on this particular issue.
If my hon. friend knew what he was talking about, he would not have used the outlandish rhetoric that he has just used to describe what has happened.
My hon. friend is correct. We have been trying in negotiations with the United States, with its industry, with the government, with the unions, to get support in the United States for some type of arrangement which reflects the integrated nature of the steel industry in the two countries. We have not been able to get that.
If my hon. friend has any responsible suggestions as to how we might achieve that, I would welcome them.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Employment and Immigration. It concerns the thousands of people in my riding who are still looking for work in Toronto.
Companies with traditional plant jobs are closing, particularly in the Parkdale area of my riding. Now employers are demanding highly skilled workers with the latest training in computers and new technologies.
I would like to know why the government has done practically nothing over the past eight and one-half years to help retrain for these higher skilled jobs. Why have unemployed Canadians been completely abandoned in the midst of our nation's worst recession?
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to give credit to the hon. member. I realize he was reading from a prepared question because he knows better than what he has just said.
Since 1990, this government through the amendment to the Unemployment Insurance Act has increased the training for unemployed Canadians by more than 400 per cent. There are $3.8 billion targeted for Canadians so that they can retrain, train and access the new jobs in this new economy.
All of these measures to help the unemployed were opposed by the hon. member.
Mr. Speaker, the minister knows that we on this side supported every measure that created jobs or retraining.
Oh, oh.

The minister should open his eyes and see the dismal state of affairs that he and his government have created. For example, if you are collecting UI today in the Toronto south management area, it takes six months just to make an appointment to see an employment counsellor. Six months, Mr. Speaker. By the time my constituents see an employment counsellor about retraining, their UI runs out and they are on welfare.
Will the minister promise to put people first and make job retraining the highest priority by providing, one, more counsellors and two, programs in the high skill areas?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is interested in scoring cheap political points. That is all he is trying to do.
Order.

If he cares so much about the people, if he cares so much about the unemployed, if he cares so much about creating high wage, high skill jobs, why did the Liberals vote against Bill C-91? Why have they opposed every measure to try and improve the lot of unemployed Canadians? The record is clear. The Liberals were against it.

May 10, 1993
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister for International Trade.
The minister will know that since 1988, 390,000 manufacturing jobs have been lost throughout Canada, and in Saskatchewan alone 6,500 fewer people are working than in 1988. One in nine manufacturing jobs have been lost, and even in the service industry jobs are down.
I want to ask the minister when will he admit that his government's economic policies and its commitment to the free trade agreement have failed Saskatchewan? When will he change direction? When will he start putting Canada first?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for the past eight and a half years this government has been putting Canada first.
If my hon. friend would reflect on what happened last week under the free trade agreement he would see the benefits of the policies of the government. With the softwood lumber panel decision we have been able to remand back to the Department of Commerce a decision which clearly the panel found unacceptable.
When there was a previous decision by the Department of Commerce of the U.S. government in 1986, we did not have that opportunity. The only thing different between now and then is the fact that we have a U.S.-Canada Free Trade Agreement with a dispute settlement panel which provides for the types of decisions that we heard last Thursday or Friday on the softwood lumber decision.

Mr. Speaker, I do not know quite what that has to do with Saskatchewan and the jobs lost in Saskatchewan, nor do I know what it has to do with the 390,000 manufacturing workers who are not working any longer. That will not fly with the workers who are now unemployed.
I want to carry on and ask the government why, when Canada has lost three times per capita the number of manufacturing jobs that the United States has lost, why
when the United States is re-thinking NAFTA, why when the Clinton administration is putting Americans first, why will not government not put Canadians first? Why will this government not put job creation at the top of its list of priorities?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International TVade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is a difference in the approach to job creation between the New Democratic Party and the Conservative government. The New Democratic Party would like to force-feed the economy with lots of money, money that it does not have, money it would like to borrow. What we have been doing on the government side is putting in place policies which are generating economic activity.
I would draw his attention to the free trade agreement once again. We had a 13.6 per cent increase in exports to the United States last year in a period of slow growth in the U.S. economy. How did that happen? Canadian industry now has a substantial margin of preference as our tariffs into the United States have gone toward zero. In 70 per cent of the cases, I believe, they are already at zero and no change with other countries. As we have that margin of preference, we have been able to increase our exports to the United States by 13.6 per cent.
If my hon. friend needs a little bit of a lesson here, a 13.6 per cent increase in exports creates jobs.

Mr. Speaker, despite the low mortgage interest rates, the 5 per cent down payment plan, the RRSP program for home buyers, the home building industry is still in recession. This indicates a general and pervasive lack of confidence not only in this government but in its policies. Thousands and thousands of construction workers are waiting at home for the government's so-called recovery to arrive and this budget did nothing for the home building industry.
I want to ask the Acting Prime Minister a question. If the government is truly interested in long-term recovery, why will it not invest in that future by forming public-private partnerships with the housing industry and get people back to work?
May 10, 1993

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I mentioned earlier in Question Period the latest statistics that came out on housing starts for April. They are up 22,300 units for an annualized rate of about 170,200 units. That is then-highest level in quite some time so we are encouraged by that.
Spending on new construction is expected to increase this year up to about $78.8 billion. It will be about a 3.5 to 4 per cent increase in building this year.
My hon. friend has lectured the government week after week, as I remember, that the answer to the housing problems was to allow a 5 per cent down payment. That has been accomplished. He also said to allow RRSP money to be used for first-time home buyers. That has been accomplished.
The hon. member is now up again saying it has not worked. Well it has worked. People have taken advantage of it. Housing starts were up in April and we are expecting them to increase throughout the year.

Mr. Speaker, the government just does not get it. People are not buying its economic policies. They have no confidence and are not buying.
The minister points to some monthly statistics. He should realize that the first quarter housing starts are down 13.6 per cent and CMHC says that only 145,000 units will be built this year which is worse than it was during the recession.
Again I ask the minister, how can the government pretend to Canadians that the economy is back on track when in fact things are actually worse than they were? Construction workers want to work. Home builders want to build homes. Canadians want to buy those homes. Why will the government not get an economic plan that will make sure people can buy and build?

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, housing affordability in Canada today is at its best point in 30 years. We have the lowest interest rates we have had in 30 years, the lowest mortgage rates we have had in years.
We are allowing people to use their RRSP money to buy homes and a 5 per cent down payment. Everything is in place. Housing starts were up 22,000 in April. Why can
Oral Questions
the hon. member not take some good news now and then?

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Acting Minister of Finance.
The budget decision to eliminate forestry development agreements will have a devastating impact on Prince Edward Island. The forest industry employs over 1,000 on the Island and has great growth potential.
Will the minister reconsider his decision to eliminate the program and support the forest industry on Prince Edward Island?

speechtext:

services.
The forestry industry is the responsibility of the provinces, as is the mining industry. The Minister of Finance gave ample notice to the provinces that these two ERDAs would not be renewed in years ahead because of the duplication and overlap. Both mining and forestry are provincial responsibilities. The Liberals cannot have it both ways.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is for the same minister.
Prince Edward Island is the only province that will not have a forestry agreement this year. One-third of the forestry jobs in P.E.I. will be lost. This is equivalent to 28,000 jobs disappearing in Ontario.
Why does the minister refuse as a matter of good public policy to put in place at the very minimum an assistance package to ease the pain of this move?

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I have mentioned it is two or three years down the road when these ERDAs come due so there is plenty of notice to the provinces to allow them to do this.
I might also inform the hon. member that his question is hypothetical. It may, it could, it might. Look, it is not going to happen. The hon. member knows that. The forestry industry will go on. We are streamlining the

May 10, 1993

operations of government to spend the taxpayers' dollars more wisely.
I know the Liberals oppose that. I understand that. We on this side of the Elouse believe we have the responsibility to streamline the services of government and that is what we are doing.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources.
With the Quebec prospectors' association, I made representations to officials in the Department of Finance and Energy, Mines and Resources Canada to stimulate mining exploration in Canada with fiscal measures. I would say that these deputy ministers understand nothing about mining exploration in remote areas.
Can the minister tell us today whether these deputy ministers will take seriously the demands of those involved in the mining sector? Do they care about the recovery of mining exploration in Canada? If so, will they submit a proper proposal? Do they understand the Quebec prospectors? If not, tell them to come to Abitibi.

speakeroldname: Mr. Michel Champagne (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Forestry
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would just like to remind my hon. colleague that the government does pay a great deal of attention to this sensitive issue. There is the Whitehorse initiative, which I discussed with the member recently. In this initiative, the federal government, the provinces, the industry and the unions got together to make the mining industry even more competitive.
I would also remind my hon. colleague that the 100 per cent exemption called "incentive taxes" still exists. I think that is something very good for the mining industry in Quebec.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Acting Prime Minister.
A month ago, Curragh Resources indicated its intention to walk away from the Westray mine in Nova Scotia. At that time, the Minister of Public Works said that this cleared the way for Devco or another operator to become involved.
Can the government explain who owns the mine and the mineral rights, especially after the federal government spent $80 million on loan guarantees on behalf of Curragh Resources?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the mine still belongs to Curragh Resources which is seeking protection before the courts under the Commercial Creditors Arrangements Act.
Canada is involved simply as a creditor. We have no further role than that.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary is for the same minister. That is not very reassuring to the people in that community who want to have some action by either the Government of Canada, Curragh Resources or the provincial government.
Yesterday was the anniversary of the death of the 26 miners. The bodies of 11 miners are still underground. The families of those miners are taking independent action to try to recover the bodies. Will the federal government assist in that operation?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member knows the provincial government appointed an inquiry to look into all aspects of it.
That inquiry has been put on hold pending criminal prosecutions initiated by the RCMP. In terms of any further action, I think that would require further progress on these legal proceedings that are under way. At the end of the day, the jurisdiction for this lies solely within provincial government constitutional authority.
May 10, 1993

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the minister of clams and lobsters.
I would like to compliment the minister for responding quickly to a clam issue and protecting the clam resource in my riding though we now have a lobster problem.
We would ask the minister to divide zone 26A in half and accept a higher carapace size for lobsters in the interests of conservation. The lobstermen have asked for this and they are agreeing to it. Would the minister consider dividing 26A in half and establishing that higher size in the interest of conservation, please?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and Minister for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency):
speakerposition: Minister for the purposes of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency Act; Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the first reasonable question I have heard during this Question Period.
With respect to the request, there has been a report called the Gardiner Pinfold Study done on the lobster carapace. A big issue, by the way, in Prince Edward Island and parts of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia is what size we should allow the carapace on the lobster to grow. Hon. gentlemen opposite have hard shells so they will understand the problem. It is quite controversial.
We just received this report in March and we are studying it. We will be consulting with all those interested and next year we will make a decision on the carapace size. We cannot divide a zone as the hon. member requests but the fishermen in his area ought to be congratulated for the position they are taking. I think they are moving in the right direction.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Acting Prime Minister.
The report released last week on harassment in the Canadian forces told us clearly that most victims of harassment do not complain. They keep quiet because they think they will be blamed and labelled as trouble makers and nothing will be done about the harassment in any case.
Oral Questions
What personal responsibility has the minister taken to make sure that action is effective and fast against harassers and those who protect harassers?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the minister of defence said last week upon release of the study on harassment, the policy of the Armed Forces is zero incidents.
To ensure that occurs, there is a three-pronged approach. There is education and training. There is a reporting system so people can be assured that any complaints are dealt with properly. There is a change in the provision of advocates or harassment advisers in terms of knowing so that people can consult and see what their rights are and how they need to proceed.
I am sure along with the hon. member, knowing the professionalism of our Canadian Armed Forces and the fact that when they do put rules in place these rules are obeyed and followed, that she should have every confidence that any problems that exist will certainly be cured and to the extent you can recognize you are dealing with human beings the situation will be as good as it possibly can be.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the same minister. That is virtually the identical answer I got from the then defence minister four years ago when I raised this issue.
Elizabeth Lafay complained of harassment and she was released from the Armed Forces. Patricia Tondreau was harassed and suffered four years of humiliation. She is about to be discharged while those who ignored her complaint continue to rise in the ranks.
Why are the victims punished and the harassers and those who protect them rewarded? Why this discrimination?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is not accurate in stating that nothing has changed. In fact there was a study, initiated by the Minister of National Defence, and a report came out last week. As a result of that report, procedures have been put in place which I just articulated to the hon. member. How she can stand in her place and make the

May 10, 1993
Oral Questions
fallacious claim that nothing has changed in four years is beyond me.
I would ask the hon. member to give more than four days for the policy to work. It was announced last Wednesday. The proper action has been taken. Unlike the hon. member, I have confidence in our Armed Forces.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport.
The minister is in possession of a consultant's report that recommends against the privatization of flight inspection services for reasons of safety. In flagrant disregard for this report the budget proposes privatizing this important responsibility.
Is the minister prepared to tell the House why the safety concerns outlined in the THA-Monenco report have been rejected? Why will he not make public both the consultant's report and the government's reasons for disregarding it?

Mr. Speaker, perhaps we are reading different budgets.
The answer today will be the same as I gave to the same question last week from the same member and that is that we have different opinions from different people on this. Safety of Transport Canada aviation is of the utmost importance. We are trying to achieve the same result in safety by looking at different alternatives. The alternative of privatizing part of the aviation inspection service is being looked into. No decisions have yet been taken.

Mr. Speaker, I think it is of vital importance that the public be given the reports and the reasons for the government's actions. The THA-Monenco report says there are too many risks involved in an out-sourcing proposal for flight inspection services.
Why would the Minister of Transport, given his responsibility for the protection of public safety, allow this measure to proceed in the face of safety concerns? Is this another case of someone other than the Minister of Transport making transportation policy for Canada?

Mr. Speaker, I repeat that no decision was made and that we are examining this issue, keeping in mind that safety is first and foremost. Everything we do will be done with safety in mind and we will examine every possible way of providing the same service to the public, with the same level of safety, if we can save Canadian taxpayers money.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Employment and Immigration.
A few weeks ago it was reported that a federal learning strategy had been prepared by five departments for cabinet. This strategy would increase the role of the federal government in education in part by giving Ottawa the lead to set national standards. As I have said several times in this House, the federal government should play a leadership role in this area and respond to the concerns that Canadians have about our education system.
I ask the minister: At what stage is this proposal and when will it be made public?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the federal government will soon outline its plan to respond to the prosperity action plan which was completed by the private sector. It is important that at the federal level we respect fully the role and the responsibilities of the provinces in matters of education. This federal government wants to support all Canadians so we can meet the learning challenge that we all face as a nation. The plan we are working on will take that into account.

Mr. Speaker, the question of what to do about the pensions of members of Parliament has been brought up repeatedly over the last few years. With the latest developments in Alberta and possibly other provinces, taxpayers are anxious to see changes in the House of Commons.
May 10, 1993

My question is for the President of the Treasury Board. Will changes to the pension plan be introduced during this session of Parliament?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for her question.
As members know, some months ago the government initiated a very extensive review of all of the federal Public Service pension system. We made excellent progress. We had in this House Bill C-55 which achieved good progress particularly with respect to a fairer deal for part-time workers, mostly women, and a fairer deal for correctional service employees.
We had royal assent toward the end of the year. We have been implementing these measures. I said at that time that in the second phase we would look at the remuneration of members of Parliament. We are now there. I have asked officials from Treasury Board to come forward with proposals and they have. In the next few days I should be in a position to announce the next step.

Mr. Speaker, I would just as soon not have to ask this question but I feel compelled to ask it of the Acting Prime Minister.
While Canadians are struggling out of the recession from coast to coast to coast, with disposable incomes dropping and levels of employment increasing, all of the Conservative leadership candidates indicate that it is important that the Prime Minister lead by example.
Over the weekend we were all subjected to the picture of the Prime Minister with Boris and the boars. I want to ask the Acting Prime Minister: What kind of example does he think it is setting for the people of Canada when the Prime Minister of our country during these very difficult times is off on a hunting and fishing trip?

question you want to put should not be put, you should probably follow your instincts. It is too bad the hon. member did not do that.

It would also define the term obscene in the Criminal Code to include material that portrays explicit sex coupled with violence, undue exploitation of sex that degrades or dehumanizes a person or explicit sex employing a person who is under the age of 18 years of age. Mr. Speaker, I am glad you specified that the 10-minute maximum remaining was in the debate.
I spent the first 10 minutes allowed before Question Period dealing with the matter of co-ops, how the GST has been a particularly onerous burden on them and how the bill before us simply does not address that problem.
I would now like to turn to the general aspects of the GST and briefly set out the reasons why the NDP caucus remains irrevocably opposed to the GST.
First of all it is a regressive tax. There can be no doubt about that. When Peter Pocklington goes into a Pizza Hut in Edmonton and orders a pizza he pays exactly the same GST on that pizza as the poorest resident of inner city Edmonton does. It can be argued that the poorest resident of inner city Edmonton gets GST rebates that take that into account.
The problem with that retort is two-fold. In the first instance there is ample evidence that the rebates being paid out simply do not cover the GST expenses, especially of those with larger families who wind up paying GST on most of the non-food products they purchase. Second, the poorest of the poor do not get the GST rebates because they do not stay at any one mailing address long enough. They do not file sufficient numbers of tax returns and other tax information to give the government the first clue where to find these people. It is the poorest of the poor, the most wretched, who are most heavily penalized by this tax.
Second, the way the GST functions creates a new and vastly increased underground economy and in consequence creates thousands, perhaps millions of tax cheats. The GST is turning a huge segment of the Canadian population into-I was going to say felons, but that is putting it a bit strongly-people who are flouting the tax law. This does nobody any good.
Today's Quorum contains a story reprinted from The Toronto Star of two days ago entitled, "GST cheating costs $2.3 billion a year Ontario report says". That is phenomenal and is there only because the GST is there. By continuing to levy the GST we are in a sense compelling a huge proportion of Canadians to become criminals.
Last, and this is the most telling point, the overwhelming majority of the Canadian people are still opposed to the GST. This was an unpopular tax when first it was proposed, it remained an unpopular tax throughout the entire process of its implementation and is to this day an unpopular tax.
The question becomes, if you accept these three arguments as I clearly do, as the NDP caucus clearly does, what do you do about it? Clearly you find yourself compelled to do away with the GST, but the question is with what is it replaced?
We in the New Democratic Party take that question seriously. Unlike our fanciful friends further up the aisle in the Liberal Party who believe that the best policy is no policy at all, never make a commitment you cannot keep and in Liberal Party policy never make a commitment at all. Honesty may not be the best policy. It may be that no policy is the best policy as far as Liberals are concerned.
In any event, we in the New Democratic Party have taken this challenge seriously, which is why we have incorporated into our jobs plan a thorough recitation of what we propose to do to get rid of and replace the GST.
May 10, 1993

I will go through these highlights very briefly to give the House some idea of what it is we are proposing.
First of all, it is a phased approach because to act in other than a phased approach would be to invite either fiscal chaos in the federal government or severe dislocation in the Canadian economy. We cannot suddenly turn around an $18 billion to $25 billion tax overnight. We have got to be careful in how we go about implementing the changes.
Therefore, in the first year we will eliminate the GST on a basket of products targeted to produce new jobs quickly. This basket includes new homes, books, children's clothing, furniture and the like. We estimate that this will reduce GST receipts by about $2 billion over a full year and by this measure alone we would generate 40,000 new jobs.
In the second year we would reduce the GST rate to 5 per cent which will put another $4 billion into the hands of Canadian consumers.
In the third year the reduction in the rate would take it down to 4 per cent and in the fourth year the reduction would take it down to 3 per cent. In the fifth year the elimination would be achieved and the tax would be gone altogether.
What do we replace it with? Clearly there is going to be no one simple answer to that question. The answer therefore comprises a number of different proposals including, but not limited to, such elements as removing the special tax reduction for manufacturers which now sees manufacturers paying 5 per cent less tax than non-manufacturing firms.
This subsidy to manufacturers costs about $1 billion a year. It was implemented originally in response to a U.S. subsidy for exporters. The U.S. repealed its subsidy in 1986 but at that point the Tories changed tack and decided that our 5 per cent reduction in the tax rate for manufacturers was because it was necessary for firms paying the manufacturers' sales tax.
The manufacturers' sales tax has been removed, so the raison d'etre for the maintenance of this special reduced tax rate for manufacturers has quite evaporated. Therefore the reduced rate ought to evaporate. That is $1 billion a year right there.
Government Orders
We then move to the fact that the present tax system allows businesses to deduct the cost of meals, entertainments and even escort services, deductions which alone cost the federal government about $1 billion a year. We would eliminate that deduction. There is another billion dollars.
Over half the $1 billion in revenue lost each year through the $100,000 capital gains exemption goes to the 1 per cent of Canadians with incomes over $100,000 a year. We will retain this deduction for primary residences, small businesses and farmers, but otherwise it will be gone. The $100,000 capital gains deduction for everyone else will be gone.
The tax system also allows only 75 per cent of capital gains to be included as taxable income. We will eliminate this reduced rate and instead will allow investors a reduction to compensate for the effects of inflation.
Tax laws still allow corporations to deduct the cost of borrowing money to finance investments overseas and to finance mergers and acquisitions. We will restrict this deduction and eliminate completely it as it applies to foreign investment by Canadian firms.
There is the minimum corporate tax. When you have a system in which over 90,000 companies with combined profits of over $27 billion avoid paying any tax whatsoever every year, you have a system that is out of whack. Nine billion dollars in corporate profits avoid any tax simply because of tax preferences.
A corporate minimum tax set at 14 per cent, half the statutory rate, would raise about $1 billion a year.
Further, we propose to re-jig the income tax system to restore a degree of progressivity in the system that has been utterly gutted by the current Conservative administration. This means, among other things, adding a 35 per cent tax bracket for net personal taxable earnings in excess of $88,770 and a 40 per cent tax bracket for net personal taxable earnings in excess of $118,360.
Any hon. member wishing further to investigate these proposals is invited to contact my or any other New Democrat member's office for a copy of the "Strategy for a Full-Employment Economy". We can get Canadians back to work. We can get rid of the GST. We can get rid of free trade and we can do it all without adding a penny to the deficit.

Mr. Speaker, I see there is some consternation on the part of my colleague from the NDP who is concerned that nobody is taking him up on his offer.
We know the reasons why. The government is not interested in anything, especially that which emanates from the NDP, nor is it interested in hearing anything that is backed up by statistical data. Those who might normally be taking the lead on legislation such as this have been silent both by their words and by their presence.
It is important for Canadians to appreciate the implications and the impact of the GST. Just a few moments ago the clerk of the House read the intention of this bill and how it encompasses many pieces of legislations that are included in the amendments under Bill C-112.
The most important thing to keep in mind and that all Canadians will certainly address is the implication of the GST on the Canadian economy. First and foremost, the one most damming suggestion that all Canadians keep hearing over and over is why the government imposed the GST when there was an array of other options available to it when considering tax reform.
That condemnation reverberated everywhere over the last couple of weeks and most particularly in the last couple of days as both the IMF and the Government of Ontario have pointed out to the public and to the Government of Canada that the imposition of the GST has had a deleterious effect on revenues to both levels of government. A very conservative estimate of the negative impact of the GST is that the governments of Ontario and Canada have lost something like $2.3 billion in net revenues as a result of its imposition.
Any government that is interested in increasing its revenues and looks at this kind of negative impact cannot possibly try to defend the imposition of such a tax when it stares a loss in revenue in the face.
We tried to get information for about a year. Until the public accounts came for the first year of the imposition of the GST, we had to rely on the statements of ministers, by government members and by some of the monthly statements that came from the department itself. Finally there was the acknowledgement that we raise approximately $30 billion from the GST. We draw from the marketplace, from the consumer, we tax the typical taxpayer something like $30 billion annually.
What does that translate to in net revenues, revenues that go to pay for some of the expenditures the government is so fond of saying it has put in place over the wishes of the opposition.
Those $30 billion have netted us barely $15 billion. Let me see if we can all understand what that means. The government puts its hand in your pocket and mine, takes out $1 and says it can only use 50 cents of this to pay bills. The other 50 cents it is going to give back. However, the taxpayer does not get 50 cents back because at least $800 million goes into the government's effort of sticking its hand in your pocket to take out that dollar. Tremendous.
Why did it not just leave us alone in the first place? Why not develop a tax system that is more efficient and one that would not cost the government 50 cents to get 50 cents, one that would not cost 50 cents out of every taxpayers' hard-earned dollar to get another 50 cents. From the point of view of efficiency, this has got to be one of the worst conceptions ever.
Two and one-half years ago in the debate that proceeded the imposition of the GST, when members opposite where asked what the options were that the government put aside in order to impose the GST, we received nary an answer. We got the same kind of flippant, almost semi-idiotic response we are getting today. They are asking us what is our replacement? What is our suggestion? We listed at least seven at the time. But it is not the obligation of opposition members to provide the government with options. It is the responsibility of every party in government to tell the Canadian public what are the options it discarded in order to impose the one that has been accepted.
After all, it has the resources in manpower, expertise and dollars. Canadians have been very trusting. We wanted to know what it was the government said was not appropriate in terms of tax reform that made GST so appropriate, why it was that the government could not consider or would not tell Canadians what options were available to it that would not involve hiring an additional 4,400 people in order to administer this new tax. Think about it. We had to hire an additional 4,400 individuals to impose this tax.
May 10, 1993

That is 50 per cent efficient when we add the approximately 1,600 already in place. But we are talking about why we would not be told what the costs were from the provincial side as a result of the imposition of the GST, the tax that is only 50 per cent efficient.
Worse is the condemnation by the International Monetary Fund. It is not a provincial government but the International Monetary Fund that says that it is concerned about the way the Canadians are responding to the GST. What do we have? The minister for revenue and department officials dismiss it as: "What happened is that the Canadian public reacted rather negatively to the imposition of the GST and compliance has not been as good as we had expected".
What did they expect? Opposition members told them in debates when the government imposed the GST on the Canadian taxpayers that compliance would not be very good. In fact, we pointed out that we would have a growing underground economy. Studies have been produced over the course of the last year which indicate that the growth of the underground economy has reached such staggering proportions that, on a very very conservative estimate, now includes a minimum of 15 per cent of the Canadian economy and most likely approaches 25 per cent.
Without objecting, when we listen to the arguments of the party opposite in government when it says that this is a good tax to impose, we are condoning a legislative initiative that turns Canadians into criminals. The incentive for evading taxation is such that the rest of the public says this kind of legislation is insane and therefore deserves to be ignored. We produce a very negative climate psychologically among Canadian taxpayers that says: "Why should I pay something that is so inane and so oppressive as this?"
The Canadian public takes a look at that 50 per cent inefficiency and says: "If I have to pay 7 per cent on everything I buy and on all the services that heretofore were not taxable and we are getting 50 per cent efficiency then why not at least reduce it to 3.5 per cent?" At the very least this would save an enormous amount of psychological aggravation. We would have had a Canadian public that would have been a lot more receptive to

spending on Canadian-made products and on manufacturing that would have been absolutely crucial to the maintenance of the welfare of the Canadian economy.

The minister responsible for privatization kept going on just prior to Question Period with a whole litany- perhaps the minister is in another world-of the legislative items that the opposition members on this side of the House opposed. Mr. Speaker, we have an advantage in Canada because 25 years ago, the Government of Canada decided to proceed with a genuine tax reform and set up a royal commission, known as the Carter commission. After five years of consultations and study, in 1967 the commission published its recommendations. This report was literally a revolutionary document. It argued that an industrialized country like ours should have a balanced and fair tax system and explained how to go about it. Unfortunately, the wealthiest in our country who belong to the financial elite objected strongly, and these recommendations went up in smoke.
This report contained the basics of a system that would have met the requirements of all Canadians. All levels of society would have had a fair and equitable tax system. We saw that with the Carter commission, which produced quite a revolutionary report. Even the principles of that study still apply today. If we examine the past and go through the past two elections, the Liberals actually won as a national party. We know how they did it, by deceiving the Canadian public with regard to taxation. 'They did it in 1974. In 1980 it was the 18 cents a gallon tax. They avoided that one. We do not want to go back into history but in 1980 they did it and in 1974 they did with regard to price and wage controls.
What I want to put on the record again with regard to taxation in relation to the GST is an outline of the studies recommending changes to the old federal sales tax, the manufacturers' sales tax.
Those studies go back believe it or not to 1940. The truth is we are the only government that had enough backbone to stand up in this House and actually bite the bullet. We knew the old tax was not working. Canadian manufacturers have been telling us that over the past number of years.
What we did was to take a look at this. Anyone that was aware of what was going on knew that we had a problem. It was just a question of when you actually come to grips with it or do you just pass it off to a future government?
We are going back a long way but in 1940 the first recommendation came from the Royal Commission on Dominion-Provincial Relations, the Rowell-Sirois commission. Any history student will remember that one. Back in 1940 they called for fundamental changes to the tax but no one acted on it.
In 1956 another committee, a small group called the sales tax committee, was established by the then minister of finance. It recommended that the basis of the tax be changed to the level at which retailers purchase goods wholesale. Again in 1956 changes were recommended.
The same thing occurred 10 years later in 1966 when the royal commission on taxation, the Carter commission, called for replacement of the tax at the retail level.
In 1975 another recommendation came down from the Department of Finance in a Department of Finance discussion paper on federal sales and excise taxation
Government Orders
recommending reform of the structure of the federal sales tax system and identified alternatives.
In 1977 the same thing, the report of the commodity tax review group. Officials of the Department of Finance and Revenue reviewed the discussion paper and suggested uniform application of the federal sales tax at the wholesale level as a practical and effective solution to the problems of the current FST.
In 1983 the same thing, the report on the federal sales tax review committee, the Goodman committee appointed by the Minister of Finance, recommended further study of shifting the federal sales tax to the consumer level. Obviously that is what we did.
In 1987 the white paper on sales tax reform indicated the government would implement a multi-stage sales tax as part of the comprehensive tax reform. In 1987 in the 20th report of the standing Senate committee on banking, trade and commerce, tax reform in Canada called for replacing the federal sales tax with a broad based multi-stage tax like the GST.
In 1989 the goods and services tax technical papers pointed out the benefits of the proposed GST over the FST. In 1989 the report of the House of Commons finance committee recommended replacing the FST with the GST.
There we have it, a litany, a history of proposed changes to the old federal sales tax, the manufacturers' sales tax. Most of us on this side of the House will admit that it has not been easy because to effect change is never easy. It is always politically risky but we did it. We did it based on recommendations going back to 1940. We faced up to that reality. They do not understand that the old tax was broken. It was hurting us in terms of export and the international capacity to compete. They do not understand that.

One of the reasons for that is because we have not shirked our responsibilities. When it comes to taxation and managing the economy we have done what had to be done and will continue to do that. The folks across the hall do not like it but it is clearly on the record for them to look at.
