If we want to refer to the international think-tanks or the IMF or look at what some of the Canadian banking economists are saying about the Canadian economy, they will say that we are doing very, very well in a western world that has been plagued in the last number of years by a very deep recession. We are moving out of it, but we are not going to move out of it by going back to the old ways of doing business.
We have laid our cards on the table and they are there to examine, but the important thing is that the Canadian people know exactly what they are. We cannot say that about the other side of the House.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member for Eglinton-Lawrence.
Be gentle.

Mr. Speaker, my colleague from Broadview-Greenwood says to be gentle. With regard to the invitation of the member who just finished, who said that having laid all of the cards on the table perhaps we ought to read them, if he will forgive me for a moment or two I will read them.
I am going to cite, just as a preamble, a letter by his own colleague from Mississauga South who during the goods and services tax debate sent out a letter to all of his constituents to demonstrate to them what the significance of the GST was. I am a little bit embarrassed to engage in such language but I do it only in an academic sense. In his words the GST was the gouge and screw tax. That comes from somebody from the Tory backbenches.
However I want to take a look at the record, since the member went to 1968 and took great pains to establish an historical precedent. I want to just look at the last few years. I said a few moments ago that I wanted to give some credit. The credit is that there was growth in the Canadian economy. It has increased by about 54 per cent since 1954. I say that because it is important for all members to understand the context in which some tax legislation can be implemented and government initiatives can be put into effect.
In that kind of a context it is important to note that the member's government opposite caused, allowed, permitted, witnessed or encouraged an increase in the public debt of 150 per cent. At the same time, we have to remember that there was an increase in the GDP but
Government Orders
there was also a 123 per cent increase in personal income taxes. So the government was getting some revenues to pay off its debts but obviously did not do it. There was a 57 per cent decrease in energy taxes at the same time. There was a further 33 per cent decrease in corporate income tax.
I do not want to overly discourage the member opposite but the trade balance dropped last year to 47 per cent of where it stood in 1984. Through all of that, because this is an example of good management, in 1988 and 1989 his government found $832 million in cash to give to oil exploration companies at a time when the oil business was booming. His very responsible members found $832 million, not including subsidies and other incentives, to give to oil companies for exploration purposes.
This member wants to compare statistics. I dare say he would pale if we kept this up.

Mr. Speaker, the statistics do speak for themselves. When the member talks about the deficit going from approximately $215 billion or $220 billion to $415 billion or $420 billion he is absolutely correct. If he wants to put numbers on it we acknowledge those.
What he has to acknowledge at the same time is that it is simply interest on the debt. Compound interest over nine years took it from approximately $200 billion to approximately $400 billion. One does not have to be a mathematical wizard to measure that.
Between 1968 and 1984, and I know they do not want to be reminded of this but I will, they allowed the deficit to go from zero, and we could argue whether it was zero or $1 billion depending on what part of 1968 we measured, to $38 billion. In my books that is a 3,800 per cent increase. In terms of the combined deficits for the total debt load, that increased slightly over 1,000 per cent.
I do not think they have too much to be proud of, but that is past history. We cannot go back to 1968 or 1984 and fight that election all over again. I suppose it would be fun to do it. We are dealing with the here and now and that is what the Canadian people will measure us on.
We will admit that we have not done everything perfectly because if we were perfect human beings there would be no need for Parliament. The nation could run

May 10, 1993
Government Orders
without us, and one could argue that it might run better without us anyway.
We will have to run on our record and we will. It is one that I think we can be proud of after close examination.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask a question of the member and I would like to deal with the here and now. I would like to deal with an issue on which the member and I both agree. It concerns the Small Businesses Loans Act.
Both of us have stood in this House several times and agreed on the fact that the Government of Canada should be communicating to small business that the Small Businesses Loans Act is out there. If we can get small business going then that is where our jobs are going to be and that is going to ultimately help the government in the record it will be putting forward to the Canadian people in the next four months.
We have two senior ministers of the Crown here today. What is causing this government to not honour its word and communicate the Small Businesses Loans Act progressively and actively? It is something that all parties in this House agree on and the government made that undertaking four months ago.

Mr. Speaker, we did make some significant changes to the Small Businesses Loans Act and it is one measure that the member opposite did support. They are major changes and we are very optimistic that they will work and they will be honoured by the banks. The minister for small businesses has had some talks and discussions and has applied pressure on the banks to respond, and they are.
As evidence of that, I want to point out that back home in New Brunswick our unemployment rate is almost below that of the national average. It is approximately 11.3 per cent as I speak, which is remarkably low for a poor province like New Brunswick. I think we have had a hand in that.
Last Lriday it was my pleasure to open Utopia Labri-cating Ltd. It is a small company back in Charlotte county in New Brunswick that is employing 50 people. It looks like it is going to expand to close to 100 employees this year. It has developed a process for recycling used motor oil. It is an environmentally friendly company and
it is competing internationally. They are also friendly people.
The evidence is clearly on the record that it has used some initiatives by this government to do exactly what it has done, which is to expand and compete internationally. It is doing so much to the benefit of every worker in the province of New Brunswick.
What I am saying in a rambling manner is that our policies are working. The Small Businesses Loans Act is working. The numbers in New Brunswick clearly indicate that it is working.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to speak on this legislation, Bill C-112.
I find all the discussion about the GST and the manufacturers' sales tax very interesting. It is as if these were the only two choices that this country had. I will grant that the Tories are right about one thing, which is that the manufacturers' sales tax was a flawed tax. It was not a particularly beneficial tax to Canadian manufacturers.
To say that the GST was the only alternative is absolute hog-wash. The government has removed one flawed tax and introduced a second flawed tax that is probably even worse than the manufacturers' sales tax. Now it is trying to play with it, to massage it and see if it can improve it.
Before I was elected I was involved in helping a number of non-profit associations develop various types of residential facilities. We would often go out in the community and purchase a building and then bring it up to standard. We might have had to put in some heavy duty wiring. We might have had to put in smoke alarm systems and even improve sprinklers. However the fundamental thing we had to look for initially was whether the structure of the building was sound. Could we make the improvements on it? Or were we simply making improvements on a building that was about to collapse or be abandoned or that was not worth the effort to improve.
That is what we have with the GST. We have an unsound tax that is rotten to its core. The government may put in all of the little improvements it wants to try to say that it is going to improve that tax, make it easier to understand, make the collection of it easier, make it less complicated, exempt this good or exempt that good, or
May 10, 1993

play around but it is left with the simple fact that the GST is an unsound rotten tax that is not supported by the Canadian public.

speakerposition: Minister for the purposes of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency Act; Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext: What is your alternative?

We have set out many alternatives and we continue to do so. If the hon. member would just sit down and listen I will set them out again in a few minutes. I know it is necessary to spell it out repeatedly for the Tories, as we have done. Unlike the Liberals we have actually set out in writing how we would do away with the tax. I will get to that and I am sure the hon. member will be in his seat listening attentively and maybe even taking notes for his cabinet colleagues.
This GST has been devastating to our economy. I come from a border community. The GST coupled with this government's high interest rate and high dollar policy has caused cross-border shopping that has devastated our retail trade. Our retail industry has suffered greatly because of the GST. People have gone down across the border particularly when our dollar was higher. As our dollar sinks lower, of course, it gets less and less attractive to go down across the border with the United States.
It has been a very inefficient tax. It costs as much to collect as the tax that is collected. That is exceptionally inefficient. The cost is not only directly to the government in a big bureaucracy. The bureaucracy is probably going to grow because now we are starting to hear about the people who are avoiding or evading or cheating on the GST. The government's solution to that will be to bring in more tax inspectors and get more people out there in the field to try to see if it can hunt down those people who are using the informal economy to avoid paying GST.
The cost of collecting the GST is enormous and it is a non-productive cost. This government is always talking about cutting down the size of government. Here is an area in which one can cut down the size of government and do away with the whole GST bureaucracy. Just get rid of all those positions and collect the tax through much more efficient areas.
Thlk to small businesses and one hears about the hassles they have had in keeping track of the GST to know what they have to pay. People talk about inputs.
Government Orders
They keep track of inputs they had so they can deduct those inputs from the GST they charge their customers. Large corporations with tax lawyers and accountants can retool the cash registers, computers and all those things. It is very nice. However, small businesses earning over the $30,000 or $35,000 exemption level have increased difficulty in keeping track of the GST. There are many other things that the government refuses to acknowledge. There are businesses and organizations that cannot collect back their GST.
I will give an example. All sorts of day care services have to go out and buy equipment, materials and supplies and pay the GST on all of it. However, they are not able to pass that on because day care is a GST exempt service. All they had to do was to eat the increase costs that they had from the GST. They could not even pass it on as a business or an organization.
I do not know why the Conservatives do not understand this. What do these places do if they increase their expenditures on all goods and supplies to 7 per cent and they cannot pass it on? The business becomes less profitable. They have to reduce wages or they have to increase the charges for day care.
Pass it along.

Yes, that is right, they pass it along to working mothers and to the working poor. That is right. They pass it along. Has that been helpful to single parents who have been trying to get out and find employment to have to all of a sudden pay increased day care costs? This is a fundamentally flawed tax. It is rotten to the core. It is like a house with dry rot in it. It is going to collapse because it is not sound.
Yes, one can spend all sorts of time and energy trying to improve it. One can put in new wiring, a sprinkler system or smoke detectors but the house is still rotten. One is better off demolishing the house and starting over again. Instead of trying to improve a rotten tax this government should be abolishing it and starting over with a fair taxation system.
I am going to talk in a minute about some of the alternatives to the GST that we as a party have outlined. However, there are other little things that I find interesting in this bill that makes one scratch one's head and wonder why the government is going ahead in trying to

May 10, 1993
Government Orders
make sure that there is not adequate information available to the public about the GST.
This bill makes it more difficult to get information because it gives an exemption under access to information. The information commissioner stated veiy clearly that he does not see the need for special GST exemption. It is simply being used by the Conservatives to make sure they have some power to hide the reality about how rotten the GST is, how cumbersome it is to collect, how much money is being spent on its collection, how many people may be avoiding the GST and how many people may be using the alternate economy or the underground economy to avoid paying the GST.
We heard the Liberals talking about the GST. I must say I am like the government in that I find it very interesting that they condemn the tax but do not have the fortitude to get up and say what they will replace it with. They talk about having a service and goods tax. It sounds like a GST but only it is an SGT. Perhaps they will have a business transfer tax which is the same as the GST only it is hidden. It is even more insidious than the Conservative one because it would be hidden from the taxpayers who could not even find out what they are paying. It would apply to a wider range of goods that would include food. It would possibly even apply to health care products and prescription drugs if we have a business transfer tax.
The Liberals waffled and said: "We will get rid of the GST. No, we are going to keep the GST. No, we are going to modify the GST. No, we are going to come in with a different tax proposal of a business transfer tax or a valued added tax or an SGT tax". Now they have the gall to say to Canadians: "We are not going to tell you what we are going to do until after the next election". They think they are going to form the government.
I have news for them. I go out into my community and talk about the terrible economic mess that the Conservatives and Liberals have left this country in and about the goods and services tax and the stand that the Liberals take. They are not going to form a government.
This afternoon again I see them having this little love-in among themselves with a new tax thing that they all support called a flat tax. This is where people who are earning $100,000 a year get their taxes reduced and those
people earning $15,000 a year get their taxes raised and we call it flat. It is like a flat earth and that is about as far as it is going to go in this country. We have already had 15 or 20 years of the Liberals trying to make a flat tax by reducing the tax for the wealthy and the corporations and increasing the tax for the poor and the working and middle classes. They started to move toward a flat tax but I think there is no-
It is a single tax.

It is a flat tax or a single rate. They have all sorts of little gimmicks in talking about it but they want to reduce the taxes further for the corporations and their wealthy friends and make the poor and the working person pay even more. This is the Liberal approach that they carried on when they were in government and then has been carried on in spades by the Tories.
Let us take a look at some of the things we said we would do to replace the GST and make it a fairer tax. I am going to just start off with two or three things.
We said let us restore some of the progressive income tax rates. How does one justify that for the wealthy tax rates in this country have gone from 44 to 34 to 29 per cent? How does one justify something like that to the person who is earning $35,000 and $40,000 a year and trying to pay for his home, feed his family and maintain some type of education fund so his kids can go to school?
Let us bring back and restore some of the progressive tax nature and let us make corporations pay their fair share. We have thousands of profitable corporations in this country that make huge profits and pay no taxes. I was looking over a list the other day and I was surprised that such outstanding corporations as Coca-Cola in 1990 earned a $28 million profit and paid no taxes. In fact it got a $1 million tax credit. People will say that if one taxes them that they are going to go across the border. I think if Coca-Cola decided they were going to stop selling coke in Canada then they will go back across the border.
Get a Pepsi.

Get a Pepsi. Certainly they can afford to pay taxes just as others can. The whole thrust of the reduction of corporate taxes in this country since the
May 10, 1993

early 60s has meant that corporations have paid less and less and the individuals have paid more and more.
However, there are many other things that we said we could do to make our tax system much fairer. There is the capital gains tax. Well over 50 per cent of the capital gains tax exemptions in this country go to the richest 1 per cent of the population. We say that there should be no exemption for capital gains other than for family farms and small businesses and private residences that are lived in. This would bring in considerable amounts of money and would allow for fairer taxation and doing away with the GST.
There are the business entertainment tax and meal tax exemptions. Businessmen can write off their lunches, escort services and boxes in SkyDome. The Vancouver Canucks I know will win the world series. The world series of hockey is called the Stanley Cup. One of the things that they are in the process of doing is building a new stadium in downtown Vancouver. I would bet a substantial chunk of that money is going to be raised through tax loopholes of selling boxes to the multinational corporations.
What have you got against tourism?

This is tourism financed by me, the pockets of the single working parent and tax loopholes to the wealthy. That is the Liberal way of doing it. That is not the way I would do it.
We have all sorts of others. We had the Liberals set up family trusts for the most wealthy families in this country. They were exempt from paying taxes on the capital gains portion for 21 years and when they were about to have to pay that tax what did we have? The Conservations came along and bailed out their friends. Other things such as the business advertising subsidies and the whole dividend tax credit are among many areas in which there have been tax loopholes built in for the rich and the powerful.
Take RRSPs. The government two years ago came along and said to the man who is struggling on less than $45,000 a year, you are going to be able to contribute and get a tax write-off on the RRSR Your rate will go from 20 per cent to 18 per cent, but you, the person over there that is earning $86,000 a year, we are going to increase
Government Orders
the amount that you can contribute. Of all of the unfair tax loopholes, the RRSP, the person earning $86,000 gets $500 back from his tax. The person earning $20,000 gets $220 back.
I just want to finish by pointing out that the way the government must deal with fair taxation and the deficit is to get employment under control.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Marc Robitaille (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to the comments made by my colleague from the New Democratic Party

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Prime Minister; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance; Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)
speechtext: That is not true.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)
speechtext:
The hon. member from Quebec-Est says it is not true.
In the end, it is unfortunate that the hon. member from the New Democratic Party made a 20 minute speech without referring to the fundamental aspect of Bill C-112 which, following extensive consultations with retailers and several activity sectors in Canada, proposes to improve, at the administrative level as well as in other respects, the goods and services tax. Whether it is the members of the tourism industry, taxi drivers, exporters, housing and building promoters, farmers or auctioneers, this bill will simplify the whole operation of the goods and services tax. It is unfortunate that the hon. member did not refer directly to the provisions of this legislation. Indeed, all he did was to wax eloquently on the fact that, from an ideological or philosophical point of view, he is opposed to the GST.
The hon. member says that the Liberal Party wants to replace the GST, but he does not know what would replace it. He also refers to a double language and a new taxation system. During the member's speech, we heard a lot of rambling that had neither head nor tail, but we never heard a word about the significant improvements which Bill C-112 will bring and how beneficial it will be for all those in the activity sectors which are affected.
My question to the hon. member is very simple. Does he agree that Bill C-112 will simplify the administration and the management of the GST for retailers, for cab drivers, and for a whole slew of people in other sectors? As regards the provisions of Bill C-112, does he agree that, based on a taxation system, namely the GST, we are

May 10, 1993
Government Orders
proposing today a bill which will simplify that system and help those who must operate within the present tax system? The hon. member certainly has the right to disagree with the GST, but today we are discussing a bill which improves the situation and which will be helpful. Will the member oppose or support those improvements to the GST which will be helpful to a large number of sectors in Canada?

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased that the member asked the question because I thought I had explained that at the beginning of my speech. Basically what we have here is an attempt to improve a rotten house.
I knew when I went out to purchase a house for a non-profit society or an organization I had to make certain improvements. I could call in consultants or whoever I want. The government says it consulted with this person and that person and these are administrative improvements. You could call in all the consultants you wanted and they would say: "We should put in a sprinkler system", or "We should upgrade the electrical wiring", or "We have to improve the fire exits," but if the house was rotten what they would normally tell you to do is bulldoze it. You cannot improve something that bad.
What the government is trying to say is: "We have a rotten tax, a tax that is universally hated, that has been detrimental to the economy and we are going to make a couple of improvements in its efficiency", or as he said, in administrative detail. "We will consult with people but we will not listen to them if the consultants come back and tell us to bulldoze the house".
My area of Surrey North is one of the fastest growing municipalities in this country. It has more housing starts than almost anywhere except possibly Mississauga. It is booming. However one of the things that the builders and contractors tell me all the time is that they do not like the GST on new home construction. They do not come to me and say: "Look we want you to make it administratively simpler". They want to be able to tell the new owners that there is no GST on the new building, which some of them have been doing, but they
then get them to sign a form so that the contractor collects the rebate on the GST that he has added into the price. They do not tell me that at all. They say to tell the government to scrap the GST, not to tinker around with it and make it administratively easier, not to try to fiddle with it and pretend it is something else.
They say: "This government and this country must deal with the deficit and it must deal with the growing debt". Everybody knows that. But they also know there is only one way to deal with it and that is to create full employment.
Every person who is unemployed costs the federal and provincial governments $17,500 in income assistance, UIC and lost taxes. Even the Tories must be able to do enough mathematics to say: "If we could reduce unemployment by one million at $17,500 a crack we would go a long way to dealing with the deficit".

Mr. Speaker, I want to begin by dealing with specifics related to the bill. This is a bill where we are attempting to streamline and simplify the GST.
The amendments are in the area of retailer issues in regard to discount coupons, returnable containers and buying groups. Part of the bill deals with direct sellers. There are simplified rules to allow consistent pricing and smooth operation of tax in the taxi industry. There are simplified rules to allow more consistent operation of tax for auctioneers. There are also some areas related to farmers. Rules are changed to allow feed lots to be treated the same as other vendors of feed.
Three years ago the government received many of the recommendations that are now part of the GST process. In other words, when hundreds and hundreds of groups from all across Canada came to the finance committee to make recommendations, many were ignored. But we see here with about three or four months to go before the election that the government is attempting to streamline the GST.
It is no secret that we as Liberals if we are given-and I say it humbly-the trust of the people in the fall, the GST will be scrapped.
May 10, 1993

I cannot figure out where this government is coming from. The member for Carleton-Charlotte in New Brunswick is here today. I want to read two short sections of the bill to him. I want to be very specific because we are talking about simplicity. This is section 235 and it defines the net tax for a passenger vehicle lease. This is the simplified GST and I put it on the floor for all Canadians to judge its simplicity. Section 235.(1):
Where, in a taxation year of a registrant, tax becomes payable, or is paid without having become payable, by the registrant in respect of a supply by way of lease of a passenger vehicle and
(a)	the total of the consideration for the supply that would be deductible in computing the registrant's income for the year for the purposes of the Income Tax Act, if the registrant were a taxpayer under that Act and that Act were read without reference to section 67.3 thereof,
exceeds
(b)	the amount in respect of that consideration that is, or would be if the registrant were a taxpayer under the Income Thx Act, deductible in computing the registrant's income for the year for the purposes of that Act,
there shall be added in determining the net tax for the appropriate reporting period of the registrant an amount determined by the formula A times B times C
where
A is the ratio obtained by dividing that excess by that consideration,
B is the tax paid or payable in respect of that consideration (other than tax that, by reason of section 170, may not be included in determining an input tax credit of the registrant), and
C is the proportion of the total use of the vehicle that is used in commercial activities of the registrant.
That is simplicity?
Let us talk about instalments on the food and beverage industry, section 237:
Where the reporting period of a registrant is a fiscal year or a period determined under subsection 248(3), the registrant shall, within one month after the end of each fiscal quarter of the registrant ending in the reporting period, pay to the Receiver General an instalment equal to 1/4 of the registrant's instalment base for that reporting period.
(2) A registrant's instalment base for a particular reporting period of the registrant is the lesser of
(a) an amount equal to
(i) in the case of a reporting period determined under subsection 248(3), the amount determined by the formula A times 365 over B
where
Government Orders
A is the net tax for the particular reporting period, and
B is the number of days in the particular reporting period, and
(ii) in any other case, the net tax for the particular reporting period, and
(b) the amount determined by the formula C times 365 over D where
C is the total of all amounts each of which is the net tax for a reporting period of the registrant ending in the twelve month period immediately preceding the particular reporting period, and
D is the number of days in the period commencing on the first day of the first of those preceding reporting periods and ending on the last day of the last of those preceding reporting periods.
The government defends this as simplicity? Does it not understand what small business is crying out for?
Small business in this country is crying out for less red tape. It is ciying out for an efficient tax system. It is crying out for a fair tax system. It is ciying out for something that works.
I say to you, and I am sticking with the bill, there is no way. I defy you. I will tell you right now that we will go door to door and store to store. I will go in any riding in this country. You show me how you defend that in the name of simplicity, efficiency and fairness. That is the whole problem. You people have lost connection with what is happening out there. It is this type of red tape that is just driving people crazy.
The member from Cambridge talks about the manufacturers' sales tax. I agree with him that the manufacturers' sales tax was not the best tax. Do you know that the manufacturers' sales tax was only applicable to 76,000 businesses in Canada?
What the Tories did was take the manufacturers' sales tax which they increased, by the way, four times since they came into power. If they were so upset with it they should have scrapped it right off the bat.
Do they know what boggles my mind and boggles Canadians' minds? They had 76,000 people involved in the manufacturers' sales tax and what did they do? They scrapped it and put in a GST where there are 1.9 million registrants they have turned into bureaucrats.
Do you know what a small business person has to do in order to get through the GST? He now has to hire an accountant. I have to tell you something. Do you understand what I just read? I will tell you if you

May 10, 1993
Government Orders
understand what I just read, you are a heck of a lot better than most small business people.
Most small business people who I know would admit openly and honestly: "I do not understand". In fact most accountants are openly admitting today that the current tax act of Canada is so unintelligible that even many of them who have been trained to give counsel and advice are no longer sure what some of the interpretations of the law are.
Therefore, my leader stands up and says that in the first year we are going to get rid of the GST, unlike the NDP which says it will take five years. It is pretty presumptuous to think that even if it did form a government it would be around for five years. That is a bit of an insult.
Tradition shows that the normal mandate in this country is four years. This heading into the sixth year is a very unusual phenomenon. The point here is that we are in fact going to get rid of the GST.
I have to clarify some misstatements that have been put forward on the government side and by the New Democratic Party today. What the leader of my party has said and has said repeatedly and it is not always reported is that we are going to take the first year and listen not only to Canadians from coast to coast about alternative tax systems in this country, but we are also going to listen to the provinces.
This is another problem with this current GST. It is not a harmonized system. It is a two tiered tax system that has created bureaucrats out of everybody in this country. It is unlike the traditional Tory ideology as I knew it that wants to turn everybody into bureaucrats. It is beyond comprehension why they went ahead with this.
At any rate the point is we are going to listen to alternatives. I do not know of anyone in Canada who really wants to defend the status quo. The only people I run into who want to defend the status quo are the few people who are benefiting by the status quo.
Two years ago, there were 2,200 foreign multinationals whose retained earnings were in excess of $25 million which did not pay any income tax in this country. I am not talking about companies with losses carried forward. I am talking about companies that had tax preferences built into the tax act over a number of years.
Those companies resist change. They do not want the status quo changed. They want it to stay the same way it
is.	I believe that most members on that side of the House believe that all those tax grants worth about $40 billion to $50 billion given to major corporations in this country should be re-evaluated in terms of meeting a public policy objective. That is number one. That particular aspect of the tax act has to be re-examined.
What about the underground economy? The government's former minister of revenue, now the Minister of Communications, said in 1985 that the underground economy, the cash economy, the alternative economy during the period pre-GST, was approximately $45 billion with a loss to the treasury of about $9 billion. That was in 1985.
Some experts say today that it is in excess of $100 billion. When you have an underground economy like that, does it not say that the status quo is not working. Why do people go underground? They go underground because the system is so unfair and so complex. That is an issue that has to be addressed. We are going to have to address it. We cannot do it overnight. We are going to need the time.
What about fairness? Let us talk about fairness. Can you honestly tell me that the government supports the notion where two years ago about 7,900 people in this country whose incomes were in excess of $250,000 and some in excess of $1 million paid absolutely no income tax? They did this legally because of tax preferences that were in the system. I am not against people making money. I am not against people being rewarded for their achievement and making money. But you cannot in the name of fairness have a system where people are making that kind of money and not paying any tax at all.
Some people will say: "Well, what is the amount of tax that they would be paying?" It is not just the amount of tax that they would be paying; it is also the symbolism of
it.	If somebody is making $40,000 or $50,000 a year and feels that they are more than carrying their weight and somebody living five blocks away or next door is making $2 million and not paying any tax, the symbolism of that stinks. It hurts productivity.
May 10, 1993

That is one of the problems we have in this country related to productivity. When people do not feel they are being treated fairly, they do not work as hard. I do not just mean physically but intellectually.
You have to address that tax act in a comprehensive way in the area of fairness. I know it was a Liberal initiative which was started in 1971 when we talked about the private family trusts.
It was absolutely sick that two weeks ago we passed that bill. It has an unlimited shelf life in terms of not being able to do an analysis or an accountability of the funds in those family trusts. I am not talking about confiscation here. We are talking about fairness and we are talking about people paying their share.
What are we going to do with efficiency? The courts are backlogged with tax cases where lawyers are able to say: "Well, the exceptions and the exceptions to the exceptions are going to allow us to take another two or three years to fight or appeal this particular tax case that we have in the courts right now because the act is so cumbersome and so complex". The Auditor General said just last year that the actual forms right now for the individual are not really serving the taxpayer. This was said by the Auditor General.
I know that the Minister of National Revenue is going to great pains and lengths to try and develop a form but the bottom line is that the status quo is just not working. I believe that tinkering with it, band-aiding it and altering it is just not going to do.
I make no bones about it. I have never hid the fact. This is not my party's position and I say that openly, but in an effort to advance the debate in a constructive way on the issue of tax reform, I say that it is time to go back to square one. It is time to take that 20,000 page tax act and just scrap it and have a single rate of taxation on the personal side and a single rate on the business side.
On the personal side, unlike the remark that the NDP made, where we are saying that we want somebody that is making $100,000 a year to pay 20 per cent and we want the person making $ 16,000 a year to pay 20 per cent. That shows a total lack of understanding of what the single tax
Government Orders
is all about, not unlike the comment he made about not wanting a domed stadium. If I had the unemployment he has in Vancouver right now, I would be asking for a domed stadium because of the spin-offs it brings.
Getting back to the tax thing, with a single rate of tax we build in progressive credits: credits for senior citizens, credits for families with children, a line to make sure that charities are protected. We do not touch the registered retirement savings plan. After we put those lines in and a basic deduction, we have a single rate on a postcard size of 20 per cent. Everyone is in the loop. It does not matter whether one is making $30,000, $50,000, $100,000, $1 million. We are going to reward productivity under the single tax system. The harder one works and the more one makes, the more one has in one's jeans.
I believe personally the current system works against entrepreneurship. It punishes entrepreneurship. It punishes achievement. That is exactly what Allan Mclnnis says. He is totally behind the single tax.
Not in the foreword of your book.

Allan Lymen Mclnnis, one of the best chartered accountants in Canada, is totally behind the single tax idea. Where he and I differ, he also likes a value-added tax. He likes the GST.
The hon. member brought him up, and he is a good Tory friend who happened to endorse my book. I want to tell the member for Cambridge that Allan Lymen Mclnnis, one of the best chartered accountants in Canada who supports the single tax said that this GST was the most poorly designed value added tax on the planet. We have tax on the salted peanuts, no tax on the unsalted peanuts, tax on the warm pizza, no tax on the cold pizza. There are 355 pages of amendments. Do not tell me, Mr. Speaker, that those guys understand what those amendments are all about. There is just no way.
I have one minute left. I want to do the small business side it, of the single rate on the business side which would be 20 per cent with a small business tax credit.

Mr. Speaker, this has been an entertaining speech. As the hon. member pointed out, this is not his party's position for a number of reasons but we do not have to get into that.

May 10, 1993
Government Orders
Obviously the previous speaker recognizes the old manufacturers' sales tax. I know if we are talking about the GST in isolation I can buy into much of what he says, but we have to remember, and I know that he does and he is nodding in agreement, the old manufacturers' sales tax had 22,000 exemptions.
As the member next to me from Cambridge mentioned earlier today, under the old manufacturers' sales tax, avoidance of that tax often depended on how much money one had to spend to defend oneself in tax court. There were 22,000 special exemptions. I do want to point out-and he has acknowledged that, Mr. Speaker. He is also acknowledging that his party cannot tamper, fool or change. He is suggesting that if we are going to do something, ditch it completely.
I also want to point out that of the 1.7 million businesses that are registered to collect the GST, 80 per cent of those businesses are eligible to use the simplified accounting methods, which they do. Also, about 90 per cent can choose to file only one GST return per year.
In terms of the technicalities of Bill C-112, it is an attempt to simplify some of those areas, as pointed out. The difficulty is that society today unfortunately is more complicated than it should be and I guess we can blame all levels of governments for that. This is an attempt to simplify the act. I think it will go a long way in simplifying the act and hopefully the members can support it.

Mr. Speaker, I want to clarify my remarks when I talk about my party's position.
I should say that the young Liberals of Canada, at our last policy convention put forward the single tax as a priority resolution. It passed on the floor of the assembly with very little objection. It is at our platform committee right now and in a responsible way we are examining all the options.
A party does not just take a position on one idea because one or two members of Parliament support it. There has to be a period of debate. One of the great assets of being a Liberal is that it allows you to be creative without being stigmatized.
The notion of advancing debate and putting forward alternatives is a healthy exercise. I say this in all
seriousness. I have received many good ideas in refining the single tax from Conservative members. The member for Calgaiy North has come up with some fantastic ideas.
By the way, I see now that the leadership candidates, the Minister of National Defence, the Minister of the Environment and the member for Etobicoke-Lake-shore in their debate in Calgary are now starting to say that maybe the time has come to think about this notion of going back to basics and having a single tax. We know that the Minister of National Defence has a race on her hands now, which I think is healthy for Canada, but it will be interesting to see what happens when they get into the tight comers, when they talk about specific positions. The members on that side talk about specific positions here. Let us see in the next 30 days what specific positions the leadership candidates take.

Mr. Speaker, one of the main reasons, in fact the main reason, I am a democrat is that I have a great deal of respect for the expressed will of the people.
In fact it is axiomatic that in a democratic society the legitimacy of government rests on the consent of those governed. We have elaborated that in our parliamentary system to include the concept of the mandate, which simply put is that those competing for election in a general election place before the people their proposals for major government action in the coming parliamentary term.
This, with luck, elicits a series of alternatives, among which a voter may pick and choose. The constraints, of course, are that unfortunately you cannot choose something from the Conservative agenda and something from the Liberal agenda and something from the New Democrat agenda. Sooner or later you have to sort through your choices and come to one final decision.
However that is the nature of democracy in our country. I would submit it is crucial to the proper functioning of our democracy that the idea of mandate be grasped and maintained.
How can the hon. member possibly justify the apparent policy of his party as regards taxation, which is surely one of the fundamental elements of government and
May 10, 1993

which currently consists of the government saying elect it and it will establish a committee. God only knows what that committee will come up with, but whatever it is the government will implement it.
How in Heaven's name can the member square that with the fundamental democratic concept of an earned and implemented mandate?

Mr. Speaker, the member made a very good point in the sense that when I campaigned against the New Democrats in the last election I campaigned very specifically for amendments to Meech Lake, against the free trade deal, against the value added tax, and we had a pretty good environmental approach. I believe those were the reasons I was elected.
In this particular campaign all of those same feelings that I had then are still with me. In the area of taxation what I will be saying to the people in Broadview- Greenwood is that I, as their member in that particular area, have this idea that I have been working on with many of them and others from across Canada called the single tax. It is not my party's position but over the course of a year we are going to see if there are other people in the country who have alternatives, and I am sure there are. If they elect me I am going to be pushing within my party and across Canada for a comprehensive tax return, and I think that is a constructive way to go. My constituents do not mind it.

Mr. Speaker, I want to compliment my colleague from Broadview- Greenwood for understanding the concept of Parliament, because a parliament is a location where we come to debate and advance issues. For him to legitimately, either as an individual or as a member of a party, advance tax reform is absolutely crucial to the maintenance of the health of this type of an institution.
On that basis I want to ask my colleague from Broadview-Greenwood how he would see the concept of tax reform and government concern, government intervention if it comes to that, in establishing a climate whereby small businesses-lespetite entreprises-and consumers could avail themselves of the kinds of generosity this Parliament gives to the banking system in order that it build up a critical mass financially, in order to lay out those loans that would make our businesses function.

We have not addressed that in these amendments but I wonder if my colleague could comment on how or why we should.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Marc Robitaille (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participe in the debate on Bill C-124.1 would like to make a few comments on this bill which is now at second reading.

May 10, 1993
Adjournment Debate
This legislation is an act to amend the Currency Act. The proposed amendments have to do with part II of this act, which defines the investment powers of the Exchange Fund Account. This account is of course the main depository of currency reserves in Canada.
This is essentially an internal management bill which will have the effect of modernizing the powers of the Exchange Fund Account. It will update and clarify the investment power provided for in the law, in view of the new opportunities that have emerged and changes that have occurred on the financial market over the past few decades. It will also correct certain inconsistencies in the present wording of the Currency Act.
By broadening the range of investments in high quality reserve assets that can be made from the Exchange Fund Account, we will effectively increase its earning capacity. This increase will immediately translate into savings on foreign exchange, which will not only help make government management and administration more cost-efficient, but, more importantly, will help achieve the critical objective of reducing the deficit.
I want to tell all hon. members of this House that these changes will in no way affect the management philosophy of the Exchange Fund Account, which philosophy bears the stamp of caution and responsibility. Our foreign exchange reserves will continue to be invested in assets of the finest quality. No further risks will be involved for credit, because new investments will be subject to the same standards as those presently governing securities and deposits.
Under the amended act as under the present one, you will only be allowed to invest in a limited number of high quality assets consisting mainly of securities issued by governments or by government-related institutions and deposits in financial institutions. The specific assets that go in those general categories will be designated by the minister so that the highest investment standards can be maintained.
With regard to the specific changes proposed in Bill C-124,1 will try not to use terms that are too technical. Basically, this bill is designed to relax certain restrictions concerning the kind of securities that can be acquired by the Exchange Fund Account and the maturity date of those securities. According to the bill, the fund would be authorized to acquire securities issued or guaranteed by governments or by governmental agencies or institutions, and not only securities issued directly by eligible governments as is the case now under the present law.
Besides, the present legislation includes some restrictions with regard to the maturity of securities issued by governments other than the United States government and by international agencies. Those restrictions would be removed, with the result that securities issued by all the governments, international agencies and eligible government institutions and agencies would be treated the same way as securities issued by the United States government.
In that respect, I would point out that most of the investments made by the Exchange Fund Account are dominated in the currencies of the industrialized countries with the strongest economy such as the United States, Japan and Germany.

Mr. Speaker, on April 22 I asked the Minister of Finance when he said that he wanted to reduce the deficit, why the government was not renewing the work permits of refugees who had previously been granted work permits, had jobs and had satisfied employers. Why was the government putting these people on welfare and unemployment insurance rolls when they had been working and paying taxes and were ready to continue working and paying taxes?
It is very difficult to understand why the government would do this. However the situation is the result of the new immigration law, Bill C-86, which was put into operation on February 1. Under the previous law, refugees were given work permits once they passed the first stage hearing. At that time there were two stages of
May 10, 1993

hearings, a first stage and a second stage. Refugees were granted their work permits at the first stage hearing.
Under the new law there is only one hearing at the end of the process. At that hearing, if the individual is recognized as a refugee, he or she is then given a work permit. That is all right. We agree with the one stage hearing, but something should have been done to make sure that those who had work permits under the first stage hearing under the previous law would have their work permits continued or renewed. However, that was not done. We warned the government during the debate on C-86 that this would happen. We tabled amendments to take care of that matter, but the government would not listen. In its ordinary arrogant way it simply ignored us and rammed the bill through as it was.
Soon after the new law came into effect on February 1, the hens came home to roost. We immediately heard of cases where refugees had obtained permits under the old law, these permits had now expired and therefore they had to be laid off. Employers who were satisfied with good workers had to lay them off because the government had no process to renew the work permits.
We raised this matter in committee twice, on February 17 and March 24. Twice at the committee officials and the minister said that this result was not intended by the new law and would be corrected, they said, immediately.
On April 22 when I asked the question, two months after from having raised it in committee, it still was not corrected. Now it is three months later and still it is not corrected. The numbers of refugees affected by this new law have been growing larger and larger every day.
The government, through poor management, lack of planning and arrogance did not take care of this when it introduced this and passed the law. So on the one hand the government says it is concerned for the deficit and on the other hand by bungling it is forcing people on to welfare which contributes to the deficit.
So I ask again today: When will the government proclaim regulations necessary to correct this ridiculous situation? I want an exact date. When will the government restore these work permits so that people who were working can continue to work and pay taxes rather than collect welfare? When will this be done?
Adjournment Debate

Mr. Speaker, as far back as February 161 asked a question of the Minister of National Defence to clarify the mandate and the mission of our UN peacekeeping forces in Bosnia-Her-cegovina. It was crucial at that time because 25,000 people in eastern Bosnia were cut off in the town of Cerska while a UN convoy of food and medical supplies was parked by the side of the road just 20 miles away and was not able to get this humanitarian aid to the people, the children and women who were starving.
At the same time the mandate of our peacekeeping forces was very confusing. The Secretary of State for External Affairs was saying that Canadian peacekeepers should take a more active role in the region. The Minister of National Defence got an additional 1,200 troops but she did not know how she was going to use them. She did not know what their mandate was. She said in her reply that the second battalion of the Royal Canadian Regiment was being deployed on the basis of

May 10, 1993
Adjournment Debate
what we call a permissible environment. What does the minister mean by permissible environment? That to me is not a clear mandate nor a clear mission given to our troops.
As I speak today we know that U.S. President Bill Clinton reaffirmed his readiness to intervene militarily. What is Canada's position if that happens? As a country which has a reputation as a trusted peacekeeper wherever and whenever we should be asking ourselves what is the Canadian position if an American-led offensive action is taken in Bosnia-Hercegovina. Canadians want to know.
Should Canada preserve its position as a neutral peacekeeper? That is a role which some country must assume once all the shooting stops and it is time to rebuild. Or do we have a moral obligation to intervene now offensively or defensively? Canadians want to know if Canada joins a military alliance the question is as to how far and do we join such an alliance if it does not have UN sanction? Under whose command? NATO command? U.S. command? We have to have a debate in this House to clarify this. How many Canadian lives are we willing to risk and would it be worth it all?
It seems to me that this government, and I am tossing my partisan politics aside because of the seriousness of this matter, is responding to the crisis in Bosnia-Hercegovina without any game plan whatsoever.
How many times in this House have we in the opposition asked for the precise rules of engagement and to this date not received any? The government has provided absolutely no assurances to the families of Canadian servicemen as to the safety of our troops there.
This is a conflict that has affected more Canadians than any other in our history, especially since the Second World War. The government forgets that thousands of Canadians, be they of Croatian heritage, Muslim heritage, Serbian heritage, have members of their immediate families in Bosnia-Hercegovina.
It is not only members in this House, it is Canadians generally, it is the families of the peacekeeping troops and it is the friends and relatives who want a full debate so that we know where the government stands.

speakeroldname: Mr. Rob Nicholson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to answer on behalf of the Minister of National Defence.
On August 13, 1992 the UN Security Council adopted resolution 770 authorizing the use of all emergency measures necessary to permit the delivery of needed humanitarian assistance in Bosnia-Hercegovina.
At the London peace conference on the former Yugoslavia the SSEA stated that given United Nations Security Council resolution 770 Canada was prepared to offer up to 1,200 additional Canadian forces personnel to the UN for an expanded UNPROFOR. On September 14, 1992, the UNSC endorsed the report on the situation and agreed to expand the UNPROFOR to protect humanitarian convoys in the areas. As a result 1,200 members based on the 2nd Battalion of the Royal Canadian Regiment were deployed in November to provide security for humanitarian aid convoys in the Banja Luka area of Bosnia-Hercegovina.
Unfortunately, the deployment in the area was refused by local authorities and the UNPROFOR was unable to negotiate a satisfactory solution. However, the battalion remained available for duty. It is in that regard that one company of the 2nd Battalion of the Royal Canadian Regiment was temporarily deployed to the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia upon a UN request to conduct observation and reporting duties on the borders.
The Canadian battalion's mandate is to increase the presence of the UN with a view to monitoring humanitarian aid in the safe area as agreed to by all parties. In order to save lives UNPROFOR is helping the parties fulfil their commitment to each other.
In conclusion, Canadian forces personnel serving in the area operate under United Nations PROFOR command and have always had a clear mandate and the foremost concern of our government is their safety.

Mr. Speaker, I am rising on a question I asked back on February 18
May 10, 1993

concerning the closure of the Canadian Forces Base Moncton and the depot that is associated with the base.
As part of history, I think a headline in The Times Transcript tells it all: "From $100 million expansion to zilch". The article goes on:
Canadian Forces Base Moncton has gone from the verge of a $100 million modernization to extinction in a matter of weeks.
Community leaders expressed shock at the base closure so soon after the Mulroney government had promised a $100 million upgrade of the base beginning in 1991.
Former Defence Minister Perrin Beatty had announced the $100 million commitment to CFB Moncton at former MP Dennis Cochrane's nomination meeting last June. The commitment was repeated by government officials during the November election campaign.
My question is related to the second announcement which resulted in the closure of the depot as well. The result is that the military facility as well as the depot have both been closed. I point out in the question I ask and the quote that I just read from a newspaper article in 1989 that this gives an idea of how this government has played with the lives of the people at that base and depot.
On February 18, 1993 the minister of defence announced that she was going to have another review of this whole decision. There was an announced closure in 1989 and another in 1992. Now in 1993 she again is playing with the people of the depot by saying to them: "I will have another review".
I asked her some very straightforward questions. How long is the review going to take? How encompassing is the review going to be? In the meantime, has the government said to stop the closure of CFB Moncton and the depot so that we can await the outcome of her review and not allow that process to carry on?
The minister was not in the House at the time and so it was answered by another minister who said in effect that the process was still unfolding. Then this minister lines up a meeting with the base and community officials who are dealing with this closure. At the last minute the minister has to leave and cannot attend the meeting. This leaves the community leaders high and dry again. A general is sent down a week later to say that the process is still unfolding, the base is going to close and not to expect very much in the way of change from the government position.
Adjournment Debate
Again, when is this review by the minister going to be completed? Has she issued a stop-work order so that the closure is not a fait accompli by the time the review is completed? Will she allow the citizens and the citizens' committee in Moncton dealing with this issue to have input into the decision? Those are the answers I would like.

speakeroldname: Mr. Rob Nicholson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the concerns expressed here about the future of the Moncton depot and the jobs of many of the hon. member's constituents are clear and understandable as is his desire for answers.
Let us remember how the issues arose. First of all, following a lengthy review of depot rationalization, the previous minister decided to close the Canadian forces supply depot in Moncton. The Minister of National Defence is very much aware of the concerns that have been raised about the decision and has agreed to review the issue.
The results of the minister's review, I can tell the hon. member in the House, will be made public. Snap decisions will not be taken. Our rationalization of DND infrastructure is important. A recommendation under review is to reduce the number of supply depots to two, one for western Canada and one for eastern Canada.
I can point out that the number of depots in this country have been on the decline from 34 to 21 to five and now the proposal to further reduce to two. Times change. Technology, methods of transportation, inventory and communication have evolved allowing us to rethink depot locations. To rationalize in this sense is to seek to reduce the overheads involved in past methods of storage.
The minister brings a fresh pair of eyes to this issue. Her review will allow a thorough consideration of the various perspectives of the decision taken and the appreciation of the complexity of this issue precludes me at this point of suggesting when that decision will be made. However when the minister is certain that viable, broadly researched options have been presented and considered, a decision will be rendered.
As the minister has stated before, the best solutions will serve the Canadian forces' needs and make the best use of taxpayers' money.

May 10, 1993
Adjournment Debate
The hon. member who has raised this issue before will not be surprised by this. He will I know await the minister's decision with great interest.

Mr. Speaker, on February 17, I had the honour and the privilege to put a question to the government concerning our native people.
As background information, I would like to quote the question I raised on February 17.
Mr. Speaker, recent events at Big Cove, at Davis Inlet and at numerous other communities across the country illustrate that aboriginal Candians are crying out for our help, yet this cry is falling on deaf ears.
In the case of Big Cove the federal government has yet to take any action on a coroner's inquest recommendation calling on the federal government to develop community-based mental health programs.
I now come to the question itself.
Will the Prime Minister give the residents of Big Cove his assurance today that he will personally take this file under his consideration and that the tragic crisis facing this community and others will receive his government's immediate action?

As we all know, the minister of health and welfare answered the question and, to tell you the truth, I appreciated the answer. It was a very sincere answer. I think he was above board with it.
I felt that in his answer there was an indication by the minister that there was a problem getting information to the proper ministry. In fact the recommendations that were made by the coroner and the request by the chief and council of Big Cove did not get to his department at the federal level. They were refused in the maritimes section.
I would like to point out at this time that in The Ottawa Citizen this past weekend there was a story that highlighted the deplorable facts that exist across Canada. It was entitled: Indian Youth Challenged. Here are some of the facts: Overcrowding in reserve homes is 16 times the national rate. Life expectancy for aboriginal peoples is more than eight years lower than for other Canadians. On reserve Indians have the lowest average personal income at one half the level of the Canadian average.
Approximately 51 per cent of all Indian children live in poverty with that level rising to 64 per cent in some provinces. Indian teens are five to six times more likely to die from self-inflicted injuries than other teenagers.
As we can see the situation as it exists in Canada is deplorable to say the least. What about the Conservative record? The hon. member will speak for the government later. If we look at the last nine years, we see that the answer to these problems has been a lot of cutbacks in various programs.
This evening I would hope that the hon. member representing the government would assure Canadians, and especially aboriginal Canadians, that these cuts will stop, that funding will be returned to former levels and that programs will be developed and implemented by aboriginal people for the aboriginal people.

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the Minister of National Health and Welfare I am pleased to inform you, and of course my hon. colleague, that the Department of National Health and Welfare is funding a suicide prevention program in Big Cove and we will continue to provide psychological counselling to all those in need. The department is also going to be helping the community fund a community survey and study into the dreadful youth suicide.
The chief of Big Cove has established a Big Cove services co-ordinating committee to ensure a co-ordinated approach to implementation of a wide range of community based programs aimed at the various factors which underlie this recent wave of suicides. Membership includes representatives of the Department of National Health and Welfare, the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, the province of New Brunswick and the Big Cove First Nation.
This comprehensive community based approach with government departments working in partnership with Big Cove First Nation is I believe the veiy best possible way to begin a solution to the tragedy of suicide in this community. The Big Cove services co-ordinating committee will also be reviewing the coroner's inquest recommendations.
To date Big Cove has accessed funds through the native component of the community mental health child development program under our Brighter Futures initiative to conduct a community-based mental health needs assessment. Future program support is available through this initiative based on described community needs.

There is $145 million available under the mental health child development component and $5 million for program parenting skills of the Brighter Futures initiative to assist communities to develop their own community-based mental health programs, using of course training of the band workers and assistance for planning and ongoing community support programs.
